speechtext:
Bill (No. 220) to incorporate the Albert and

Moncton Railway Company, was read the first time last night. With the leave of the House I propose that it be now read the second time, and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

I do not know why this kind of thing has to happen so frequently. We are not going home to stay at home for ever; we are coming back in a couple of months, and, unless there is some special reason for it, I do not think this ought to happen. I think we should all observe the ordinary procedure and not being everlastingly breaking our own rules.

I quite appreciate the fact that if any hon. member objects this cannot go through, but I would urge that consideration be given to this Bill. It is connected with a large enterprise in the county of Albert, involving the development of the shale interests in that section of the province and, expedition is necessary in order to further the objects in view. That is the only reason I would urge upon my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) to give his consent, and other hon. members to raise no objection.

I only wanted the hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) to give some reason for his motion. I do not propose to jump on his Bill in particular; a gentleman for whom I have very great respect -but I do not like this procedure as a rule, and I wanted some reason given.
I quite agree.
I heard this shale argument advanced about twenty years ago. I am afraid it comes now a litt'le late in the day.
It is a new thing there.
I can hardly imagine that the question of the Bill going through a few weeks later or a few weeks earlier would make much difference to that great interest in that county.

I may explain that English capitalists have taken hold of the matter now, and if there is delay here that will delay their movements in connection with the development of what is hoped to be a very great industry. As my hon. friend has said the shales have lain dormant for many years, and we cannot hasten their development now with too great speed.
Motion agreed to, and Bi'll read the second time.

I move:
That leave be granted to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines to sit during the time the House is in session in accordance with the recommendation contained in the 21st report of the said committee.

speechtext: I think this is entirely unnecessary. There is very little to come before that committee, and if the committee would meet, as it did to-day, half an hour before the time of the sitting of the House, there would be plenty of time for it to pass all the Bills that come before the committee. We have granted this leave in the case of two committees this session, when, in my judgment, there was no need for it. When the House was in session, most of the members desire to be here and possibly to take part in the debates that go on. But if the committee is sitting at the same time as the House, a member of the committee must make a choice which he shall attend. What is the reason for asking that this committee be allowed to sit while the House is in session?

speechtext: That is simply a scare signal thrown up. There is plenty of time for the committee without their meeting when the House is in session. I for one am opposed on principle to a committee doing business while the House is in session If there were a rush of business I could understand it; but I imagine there are very few Bills to come before the committee, and those of such a nature that they need take up very little time.

speechtext:
I desire to add my protest against the meeting of the Railway Committee while the House is in ses-

sion. A few days ago twenty or twenty-five of us were called up stairs to attend a committee meeting while the House was in session, and while the Minister of Railways (Mr. -Graham) was explaining a long resolution he had with reference to the Canadian Northern railway. I regret very much that I had not the opportunity to listen to his explanation, and I have no doubt there are other members in the same position. Besides, I think there is no real excuse for this procedure. The House has been in session for six months. Why did not these gentlemen bring forward their Bill and have it passed in the regular way.

I do not know whether this motion requires notice or not, but if it does, then I do not consent to it.

maintopic: COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES.
speechtext:
Important legislation is coming before this House constantly now, that we are on the eve of adjournment, and it is very desirable that every member should be in his place, and pay attention to the proceedings. One Bill that the Railway Committee desires to deal with is the Water-power Bill, that was before the House last night. This Bill came before the Private Bills Committee when there were only four members present; but the chairman with enlarged vision saw a quorum and reported the Bill unanimously, and the House started to deal with it last night, notwithstanding that it was not on the Order Paper.
This Bill is not of such urgent importance that it should be rushed through the House at this end of the session. It is a very important Bill, and while the .Railway Committee desires time for its consideration, it is desirable we should all be here and pay attention to the legislation going through the House. I think it would be a mistake to pass the motion presented by the chairman of the Railway Committee. The rights under the old Bill of 1903 have been forfeited, and the object of this legislation is to renew the rights granted in 1903, and which were forfeited three years ago. Why the urgent necessity, when they have not asked for a renewal for three years, and why should we seek now to rush the Bill through the House in the course of two or three days?

We had a meeting of the Railway Committee this morning Mr. HENDERSON
called at half past ten. There are one or two Bills now before the Railway Committee; both of them are Senate Bills, one the Bill which has just passed its second reading, and the other the Bill referred to by the member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe). I understand there is some urgency in respect of both of them, and there was a general disposition oh the part of the committee this morning that leave should be granted to sit while the House is in session in order to expedite these two measures. I do not think it is unreasonable; I do not think it will take a great length of time. It is a custom that has been followed every session since I have been in the House.

maintopic: COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES.
speechtext: I do not approve of the practice of the various committees sitting while the House is in session. The Railway Committee is composed of nearly every member of this House; therefore, if we are to be in our places in this House we cannot be in the Railway Committee. If we are not on the Railway Committee, we do not save any time, because when the Bill comes back to the House again we will have to go over the whole procedure and obtain in the House all the information afresh. So we are not going to save any time by holding meetings of the Railway Committee during the sessions of the House.

Mr. LEMIEUX moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 222) respecting the Na-

tional Battlefields at Quebec. He said: As the House is aware, some years ago a commission was appointed composed of Sir George Garneau, then mayor of Quebec, Sir Edmund Walker, Mr. Dennison, the Hon. Mr. Taschereau, Minister of Public Works of Quebec, Mr. Turgeon, president of the Legislative Council of Quebec, and the late Sir George Drummond. Upon the death of Sir George Drummond, the hon. member for St. Lawrence division, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) was appointed to replace him on that commission. The object of the commission was to implement what had already been done towards nationalizing what is known as the Plains of Abraham of Quebec. The House is aware that some legislation was passed a few years ago empowering that commission to acquire certain lands and farms around the Plains of Abraham, and near the other battlefield of Ste. Foy. The commission went to work very diligently, and has so far done splendid work. It has acquired practically all the buildings and lands which naturally come under the scope of the commission. There remains, however, a few lands and a few properties to be acquired, and the object of this Bill is to give the commission the power to expropriate these properties. The various estates and lands are mentioned in the first clause of the Bill. The second clause requires a little more explanation. I may say that the commission has been unanimous in reporting in favour of the acquisition of those properties. Some of them belong to the federal government, and some of them belong either to the Dominion government or to the local government. For instance, the observatory building on the Plains of Abraham is one in regard to which we do not yet know whether it belongs to the federal government or the local government, but that will be ascertained. It is also desired to acquire one of the old Martello towers on the edge of the St. Charles valley. This old tower is decaying, and it was thought that, being an old relic of the past, it should pass into the hands of the Quebec Battlefields Commission. The next clause also requires some explanation. The commission has obtained the service of the well-known landscape architect, Mr. Todd, who was employed, I think, for the embellishment of the environs of Ottawa. They have decided, under the supervision of Mr. Todd, to open an avenue from, the battlefields on the Plains of Abraham to the other battlefield on the Ste. Foy road facing the monument, as the Monument des Braves is on the Ste. Foy road. The first decision of the commission was to open and widen an already existing avenue known as the Belvedere. But that avenue was nbt in a straight line between the battlefields on the Plains of Abraham and
the Ste. Foy battlefield; so they have decided to open another avenue which will be in direct line between the Monument des Braves and the Plains of Abraham. It will add to the spectacular effect of the park when it is completed. The first project would have cost the commission a sum amounting to $19,000. By the second project which is now submitted to the consideration of the House, the town of Montcalm, one of the suburbs of the city of Quebec, has agreed to give the commission the lands necessary for the opening of that avenue. The town of Montcalm asks in return to be loaned a sum of $15,000 for a period of thirty years, at which time the town will reimburse the commission with interest at the rate of three per cent per annum. This amount will be loaned by the commission to the town of Montcalm in order that the town itself may acquire the necessary estates and lands for the construction of that road.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that this Bill should be introduced by resolution, since it contemplates a chaTge upon the revenue?

This ts not money of the government, the money required for the acquisition of these lands is already in the hands of the commission. The fund now in their hands is composed of sums received, not only from various parts of Canada, but from the British Empire at large. In fact subscriptions were received from New Zealand, from Australia, from Great Britain and from all the British colonies, as well as from the various provinces of Canada, and there were private subscriptions in great number. The amount now in the hands of the commission, I am informed by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence division, amounts to from $300,000 to $350,000. It is with this fund that the commission desires to acquire the said properties. But even though the commission desires to acquire these properties with their own fund, yet, according to .past legislation, it has to come to the Dominion parliament, because all sales made to the commission must receive the approval of the Governor in Council. Before I take my seat I may be allowed to lay on the table of the House, or to insert in ' Hansard,' the report of the landscape architect, Mr. Todd, on the National Battlefields under the control of the commission. As I said a moment ago, Mr. Todd has been engaged by the commission, and has prepared an outline of the great national park which will be one of the features of our national life. I would like the members of the House to read this report, which is not very long. I will hand it to the ' Hansard,' so that * hon. gentlemen may be able to read it to-

morrow. Later on, the commission may come to parliament for further aid, when the members of the House will have an opportunity to appreciate the demands made by the commission. The report is as follows:-
10 Phillips Place,
November 15, 1909.
Sir George Garneau,
Chairman, National Battlefields Commission, Quebec.
Dear Sir George,-In compliance with your request of last May, I have examined the Plains of Abraham and other property under the control of your commission, and that which you propose to acquire, with a view of presenting to you a general scheme or plan, the gradual development of which would seem to me to insure the restoration and permanent preservation of its impressive grandeur and historic interest, and at the same time make it available for public use and enjoyment.
With a situation unequalled and historical associations almost unparalleled, it is clear that you have in this property, where the fate of Canada and perhaps the whole continent mere than once hung in the balance, the making of a park ' par excellence.' There are other parks of magnificent views, and many places in the world over where the memory of past deeds of valour fill the soul of man with high ambitions and patriotism, but it is no exaggeration to say that in no other place can we find such grandeur of proportion, such sublime views combined with such a wealth of historical associations, as in encompassed within this park, lvhich legacy you have the privilege of handing down to future generations, with its grandeur and beauty undespoiled, and its historical interest revived and hallowed with the passing time.
To adequately describe your possessions is impossible. One must see to appreciate the grandeur of the views, one must wander at leisure over these old fields of strife, now so peaceful, and must live over the lives of these great men, who gave up their lives for their country, to begin to appreciate -what a priceless gem is this National Battlefields Park. This vast treasure house of the history which is so closely intertwined with that of Canada, with its magnificent panorama of views, you have secured to be dedicated forever to the people of Canada, and the question of how you shall make this available to those who wish to study its history or to gather inspiration from its sublime views, of how you shall plan the. necessary artificial features of the drives, walks, and shelters, without injuring its natural beauty or historical associations, is the problem which I have endeavoured to solve in the accompanying plan.
In presenting the plans, I have in several instances given numbers to drives and entrances to aid in describing the plan.
Broadly speaking the park is divided by its geography and topographical features into five distinct parts.
First, That portion from the Citadel to Wolfe's monument, which consists largely of a high undulating plateau, broken by small elevations. This portion of the park I have endeavoured to keep as natural and informal Mr. LEMIEUX.
as possible, and at the same time have avoid j<1 planting many trees, in order that it may remain as near as possible in the condition in which it was when the historic battles took place. In fact the only planting which is suggested is here and there a group of trees along the drives and walks, to break the monotony, and groups of trees massed along the outskirts of the park in order to screen out what may be inharmonious private property.
Second, We have that large area of comparatively level ground which has been for so long known as the 'Plains of Abraham.' This portion of the park it has seemed desirable to treat in quite a formal manner. It is proposed to locate the new monument at the edge of the slope about opposite the middle of these plains, and this is approached by a formal drive from each side of the park. It is proposed that these drives should be bordered by trees planted at regular distances in contrast with the planting in other portions of the park, which is of an entirely inf. rmal character. Thus will be formed a propt r setting and dignified approach for this m moment, which is to be the crowning feature >f the park. At the same time the formal art -ingement of this portion of the park preserves an extensive open spate, where parades and encampments may be held. In order to produce most satisfactory results, it would be necessary to build up a retaining wall of considerable height to form a terrace on which to place this monument, and as the plains are broken by a small excrescence in the centre, the material might be taken from this elevation and used for building up the terrace for this monument, thus obviating the necessity of obtaining filling from a distance.
Third, We have extending from the edge cf this plateau to the escarpment bordering (he river a large area of rather steeply sloping ground which is covered by a dense growth of coxspur thorn, and other small-growing native trees and shrubs. This portion of the park it is proposed to keep in perfectly wild and natural condition with walks leading through it in various directions and along the edge of the escarpment. In most places this escarpment is so steep as to be dangerous and when walks p.re laid out along here, protecting fences will be required in many places.
Fourth, We have a narrow strip of land extending from the plains to the Wolfe Cove read, and from Champlain street to the Merici property. Considered from a landscape point of view this is a charming spot, with its gently undulating topography extending to the steep cliff and open groves of lofty pine and elm, while historically it is of the greatest interest, as it was up this steep cliff in the shelter of the small point of land that General Wolfe and his advance guard climbed and put to flight the small French poste encamped at the head of the road leading up from the cove, thus gaining the key to the plains above.
Fifth, We have a small park on the Ste. Foy road, which although in itself possessing few features of marked beauty except magnificent views, is a point of great historical interest as one of the most fiercely contested positions in the battle of Ste. Foy. The distant views, rather poorly shown in photograph No. 1 accompanying this report, obtained from this park over the St. Charles valley, are entirely

different from those obtained from the other parts of the park, and are equally charming.
It has been rather difficult to design this Ste. Foy park in such a way as to provide a proper setting for the Monument des Braves, and at the same time lay out the park in a pleasing manner. The proposed arrangement, I think does this as well as circumstances will allow. By making two entrances equally distant from the monument, a certain needed formality is given, which could not be secured with one entrance, and below the monument the park is laid out in an irregular manner, whicli I think will be pleasing, and admit of its best use by the public.

The question of a suitable entrance to your park is one of the greatest importance. There must necessarily be several entrances, but there should be one principal one, so located and constructed as to give some idea of the importance of the park to which it is an entrance, and in so far as possible to be an index to the general character and associations of the park itself. This matter of a proper entrance to a public park is not given the attention in this country that it should. We often see a park with drives and walks well laid out, and with beautiful landscape, while the entrance is entirely unmarked, or else marked by some fantastic gateway entirely out of harmony with the character of the park. We recognize the importance of a well designed entrance to our buildings, and would be shocked to see a large classic public building with merely a hole in the wall for an entrance, or an entrance made out of rustic boulders, nor would any amount of interior beauty dispel from our minds this disagreeable first impression. It is equally important that a park should have a well designed entrance, it may be of the most simple and inexpensive construction, or it may be large and costly, but it should be of harmonious design and of such proportions and construction as will lend dignity to the park itself. This has always been recognized in the old country, as for ex. ample the stately entrance to Hyde Park in London. What could be more dignified or show more clearly the character of the park itself? Again take the entrance to the Bois de Bou-longe at Paris, or that gem of French parks, Parc de la Tete d'Or at Lyons, and yet these parks, beautiful as they are, have nothing to compare with the grandeur and historic associations of your Quebec Battlefields Park to act as an inspiration for the designing of an entrance.
Entrance No. 1, or Main Entrance.-The logical place for your main entrance is to be found on the left, immediately after passing through the St. Louis gate, at the side of the high Citadel wall. An entrance at this point could be made very characteristic, for you have at the east side'of the entrance, the massive time worn wrall of the Citadel, and I would suggest making the entrance really form a part of this wall, by building a wing wall slightly lower than that of the Citadel wall and at right angles to it across the west side of the present skating rink. You will see by photograph No. 2 accompanying these plans, that it would be impossible to make any kind of an effective entrance here *without removing this skating rink, but by removing it and haying an entrance occupy the whole width of this space, it could be made very effective and impressive. I am submitting with this a sketch for an entrance, which carries out in some measure my ideas of what would be effective. This sketch is not to be considered as a proposed plan, but simply as a suggestion to show the effect of such an entrance. One of the most important and effective features of such an entrance would be that the instant you have passed through the gateway you obtain a most striking and impressive view of the Citadel fortifications, which would help greatly to carry out the prevailing idea of the park. Photograph No. 3 gives an idea of what this view would be, although if the rough material which has been dumped near the rear end of the present skating rink were removed, the view would be even more effective than the photograph shows.
Entrance No. 2.-The entrance to your park of next importance would naturally be located near the present Wolfe monument. At this point it seems to me that the present straight drive leading up to the monument should be widened, and that a low entrance should be constructed, with gate piers eight or ten feet in height, conforming in character to the main entrance. As shown by photograph No. 4, the present entrance at this point is very poor, in fact can hardly be called an entrance. The monument itself is distinguished in the distance with an iron railing about it. The street between the entrance and the monument should be re-graded and laid out formally in order to unite it pleasingly with the formal arrangement which I have suggested about the monument itself. I would suggest that sufficient property be taken on either side of the entrance to allow for a double row of trees, as shown on the plan.
Entrance No. 3.-On account of its being necessary to maintain a certain amount of formality in the treatment of this portion of the park, I would suggest that this entrance be made similar to entrance No. 2.
Other Entrances.-There would be several other entrances to the park, viz., at Lans-downe, Tache, and Montcalm streets, and at Wolfe's Hill, Belvidere Road, etc., but these would hardly rank as important entrances, and could be marked by simple stone piers, in harmony with the other entrances.

In locating the drives, it has been my endeavour to keep before me three important considerations, to place them so that they do not break the pleasing continuity of the park, and disfigure it as little as possible; to make them conform as far as practicable to the natural contour of the ground, so that there will be no bad grades or disfiguring cuts and fills; and to locate them in such a way that a person is brought by the most pleasing and convenient route to the finest view points, and to the places of greatest historical interest.
Drive No. 1.-I have so designated the drive leading from the main entrance as far as Wolfe's monument. After passing through the main gateway, where one is confronted by the impressive view of the Citadel, this drive curves out into the broad valley in the rear of the drill hall, and gradually ascends the

hill, on which are located the martello towers, where a most beautiful view of the entire easterly section of the park is obtained, as shown in photograph No. 5. This view is, of course, at presently badly marred by the Dominion arsenal buildings. It is also somewhat difficult to realize or form a proper appreciation of this view because its proportions and distances are so large, and there is nothing at present to give it scale. A few well placed groups of trees would make a great difference in the view and afford the eye the necessary scale to properly grasp its proportions.
Prom the martello towers westward, the drive descends into the valley, where occurred the actual battle between the contending forces, and by a gentle curve approaches Wolfe's monument.
The present tower street, leading from Montcalm street to the monument, it would seem better to abandon and locate as shown on the plan. You will notice by referring to photograph No. 6, which is taken from the centre of tower street looking toward the jail, that this is a very poor approach indeed to Wolfe's monument. The street is laid out so that it appears to terminate in the blank wall of the jail, and it is necessary to squeeze by one corner of the jail and then descend by a sharp grade to the monument, whereas, by diverting this drive as shown on the plan, this disagreeable feature is obviated, and a pleasing drive with an easy grade secured with an approach directly on the axis of the monument.
Drive No. 2.-At a short distance from the main entrance this drive branches off from drive No. 1, and ascending gradually the ruins of the covered way forming part of the old fortifications constructed by the English army, reaches the high point known as Cape Diamond. Prom this point are Obtained perhaps the finest and most .impressive views of the whole park. The view up the river partially shown in photograph No. 7, is particularly fine. Hundreds of feet below and almost underneath one, winds the historic Champlain street, bordered by its quaint houses cut into the face of the cliff. Plowing by is the majestic St. Lawrence, bearing on its beautiful expanse an everchanging burden of marine craft, while in the distance Wolfe's.Cove and the picturesque Sillery church on its high plateau, jutting out into the river, make a picture of rare beauty. At this point the drive should be widened to form a concourse, so that a number of carriages could stand without interfering with others passing, and I would suggest also the building of a shelter at this point. Leaving the extremity of Cape Diamond, the drive should follow for a few hundred feet the old roadway, forming part of these fortifications, and still descending would approach quite close to the Citadel wall at its highest point. Here also the panoramic views are very impressive, but perhaps not as distinctly pleasing as those from Cape Diamond itself. From this point the drive would descend by a fairly easy grade and rejoin drive No. 1.
Drive No. 3.-This is rather a formal drive, extending from entrance No. 2 straight to Wolfe's monument, and then bordering the Plains of Abraham to the terrace on which is located the new monument. The grade of this Mr. LEMIEUX.
drive is almost level and will form a good approach to the monument.
Drive No. 4.-Branching from drive No. 1, this would pass through the present location of the arsenal laboratory, and following around the base of the hill would pass below the little hill east of the fulminate of mercury plant, and would then follow along the side of this fairly steep slope below the Martello Tower No. 1, and continuing would pass below the observatory, gradually ascending again to the proposed new monument. In some respects it is to be regretted that this drive cannot be carried more on the upper level and take advantage of the fine views which are to be obtained from such points as those on which are located the Eoss rifle factory and the observatory, but as this seems impossible, the drive has been carried for its entire distance along the side slope, and in many ways you will find this an exceedingly pleasing location. The views differ entirely from these to be had from the upper drives, and there is such a thick natural growth of trees and shrubbery that it will make the drive very interesting, especially if the evenness of this present growth is broken up here and there by the planting of higher growing trees. The distance that this drive follows this side slope is almost a mile, and in order to avoid its becoming monotonous, it will require careful treatment in the way of arranging vistas by planting and other means, so that a succession of interesting views will be obtained rather than a continuous panorama. The construction of this drive will be a little more difficult than that of the other drives,' as there will be a cut and fill for the greater part of the distance.
Diive No. 5.-This would enter the park at the westerly side of the Plains of Abraham and approach the new monument in a formal manner similar to drive No. 3.
Drive No. 6.-This drive would leave the westerly end of the monument terrace, and descending would pass along the brow of the cliff where Capt. Delaune and his band first ascended, and continuing along the brow of the cliff would join the present road leading up from Wolfe's Cove.
Drive No. 7.-You are particularly fortunate in being able to arrange such a fine approach to Ste. Foy park as that given by this boulevard.
Drive No. 8.-A formal drive enters this park from each side of the monument, and fiom the centre branches descend to the lower side of the park by pleasing curves and wind along the edge of the escarpment overlooking the St. Charles valley, thus taking advantage of these magnificent views.

By reference to the plan you will see that walks are shown leading to the various points of interest in the park from the different entrances. It has been my endeavour with the walks, as with the drives, so as to locate them, that they would exhibit the various features of the park to best advantage. Some of these walks in the less used portions of the park would be more pleasingly kept in turf until such time as their use makes gravel walks necessary.

Cape Diamond Shelter.-On Cape Diamond I have suggested a small shelter, as this is perhaps the finest viewpoint in the whole park, and will undoubtedly be very much frequented by those who wish to enjoy these views. In constructing this shelter, I would suggest that it be designed in such a manner as to harmonize with its surroundings, and it seems to me that the best material to use for its construction would be undressed native stone. The base of the shelter could be built entirely of this, and would practically form part of the cape itself, while if part of the piers supporting the roof were also of rustic stone, and the roof covered with red tile there could be just enough colour to provide a pleasing contrast.
Wolfe's Monument.-I do not know how far you would care to go in making i any changes in this monument, shown in photograph No. 8. The shaft itself is pleasing, but the surroundings and setting of the monument are lacking entirely in anything which make it really impressive, or which lend it the dignity such a monument ought to have. Therefore, I would suggest that a formal court or square be laid out about this monument, and that tho monument itself be raised and placed on a base of sufficient proportions to render it more impressive, and at the same time of such design as will harmonize with the present shaft.
New Monument and Terrace-The location suggested on the plan for the new monument seems to me to be the best which could be selected in the entire park. There might be some advantages in having this located on Cepe Diamond, but it would be very difficult to obtain there the necessary formal surroundings which are required to form a proper setting for such a monument, and situated as proposed, it can be seen to advantage from any part of the Plains of Abraham, and will be a distinctive landmark as seen from the water. The proportions of this park are so large, and especially as viewed from the water, that it will be necessary to have the design of this monument sufficiently grand in its proportions to crown this natural slope, and in order to do this, I think the monument itself should stand on a broad terrace from 400 to 608 feet in length, the masonry of which would rise above the existing slope at least 20 feet or high enough to provide a proper base for the monument as viewed from the river. I have suggested that the monument itself occupy the centre of this terrace, and that the terrace be terminated at either end by a low shelter.
Monument des braves.-This monument, photograph No. 9, forms a most effective termination for the approach drive (No. 7). The base of this is better than that of the Wolfe monument, but I would suggest that here also the surrounding fence be removed, and {hat a formal entrance be built about the base.

This is something which is rather outside the scope of this report, and yet the interest of the park depends so much on its history, that tablets and small monuments properly inscribed should be placed wherever necessary, but in all cases I would suggest that
these be kept low, and not intrude unnecessarily into the landscape of the park.,
Whenever the jail is removed from its present location, I think it would be a very pleasing feature to restore the Wolfe redoubt which surmounted this hill.
The old English fortifications on Cape Diamond, although not built until a number of years later, are very interesting and would seem to be worthy of being restored and preserved at least as ruins.
The two martello towers, photographs Nos. 10 and 11, situated not far distant from the Ross rifle factory, are objects of considerable historic interest, and particularly the one situated nearest the river, adds much to the character of the park as viewed from the river, and it seems to me a great sacrilege that this tower should be surmounted by the ugly water tank as it is at present, and moreover the walls of this tower are at present apparently being used as a butt to shoot at in testing rifles, and for a considerable area on the northeast side the stone has been broken away by the continual shooting. Certainly these towers are well worth preserving, and should not be used for such purposes. PLANTING.
I doubt if there is anything in the entire work on your park which will require more care in handling, or which if effectively handled, will do more to enhance the beauty and interest of the park, than the judicious planting of trees. Owing to the fact that the character of this park is so entirely different from that of the ordinary park, and also on account of the desire to retain the features of the topography as historically correct as possible, the amount of planting must be very limited, and must be confined to the borders of the park, with here and there an odd tree to give proper proportions to the views.
I have on this preliminary general plan shown the location of the trees, where it seems to me they should be placed, but before this planting is carried out the whole question should be studied in detail, and the position and variety of trees carefully considered, for the effect of this planting as it reaches maturity will do much to make or mar the appearance of the park. If you could put in the trees just as they are to look when 25 or 50 years old, it would be a comparatively easy matter, but inasmuch as this cannot be done, and the trees have to be put in and allowed to grow to maturity, it is absolutely necessary that they be carefully selected with a. full knowledge of what their effect will be in after years.
In planting in the vicinity of the Citadel, I would suggest using largely the pyramidal-growing Lombardy poplar, for no other tree can add interest to the old fortifications 8S would a few of these characteristic trees. Starting at Entrance No. 1, I would suggest just an odd two or three of these trees between the entrance and Grande Alice. Inside the entrance I would omit the planting against the Citadel wall until you come to the group shown on the plan on the higher ground. This will allow the Citadel wall to be seen to its most striking advantage. Near the entrance I have suggested massing trees and shrubs along the border of the private ' property, and this planting is continued irre-

gularly along the border of the park wherever it is bordered by such property. Along djive No. 1 are proposed a few scattered trees, which should be largely composed of broadspreading native trees such as the Sugar maple. Between drive No. 1 and the wooded slope below the martello tower No. 1, I have suggested very little planting, as it seemed to me more effective and more historically correct to leave this entirely open.
Two groups of trees are shown on Cape Diamond, and although it may be fairly questioned whether these would be historically correct or not, they will do so much towards increasing the interest of this portion of the park and in giving proper scale as viewed from a distance, that I think they should be used.	_	..	, .
The formal planting of trees along the drive leading to Wolfe,s monument, about this court, and along the drives leading to the proposed new monument can be readily understood by reference to the plan, and need9 no additional explanation.
The character of the park from the edge of the upper plateau to the edge of the escarpment is and always lias been so entirely different, that I have suggested here not only retaining the greater part of the existing growth, but re-enforcing it very considerably with the planting of larger growing trees. The arrangement of the trees along this drive will require careful study in order to properly frame in the different vistas, and in order to provide a liberal amount of shade, which is very much to be desired along this drive on account of its being on the southerly slope and sheltered from prevailing winds.
Below the proposed new monument in particular the planting requires very careful treatment in order to add to and not interfere with its effectiveness.
On that portion of the park between the iMerici property and the escarpment, X would suggest using 'largely the native white pine and cedar, in order to restore this as nearly as possible to the conditions that existed when Wolfe gained the ascent at this point.
The trees along the boulevard should he ordinary street trees, which are suitable for your climate, and of which none is probably better than the hard or sugar maple and elm.
In the planting at Ste. Foy park, the chief object will be to provide a formal setting for the monument and needed shade along che walks and drives, and to screen out the adjacent private property.

You have supplied me with a plan drawn by C. E. Gauvin, Esq., dated October 31, 1908, showing lands intended to he acquired by your commission in order to properly carry out your park plans. In addition to tlie requirements as shown on the plan, it 6eems to me quite necessary that the following property should he acquired.
As already mentioned in discussing the main entrance, it will he necessary to procure the property of the skating rink shown in photograph No. 1, in order to make an effective entrance.
Between the present Montcalm street and Wolfe monument, it would seem desirable that lots Nos. 4441 and 4442 should he acquired hack to the line shown on the accompanying plan.
Mr. LEMIETTY
The whole of this area is not absolutely required, but a large portion of it is necessary in order that the drive may properly approach Wolfe's monument, as shown on the plan, and the taking of these lots back to the suggested line makes a much better park boundary than to acquire just enough for the road, and as this entire ground is one of the most important parts of the actual battlefields, and where Wolfe fell mortally wounded, it is of much historic interest.
On both sides of the present entrance to Wolfe's monument it will he necessary to acquire the private property and to tear down the two rather poor houses at present standing here, and shown in photograph No. 4, in order that an effective entrance may be made.
On the Gauvin plan above mentioned, you show a line through the Merici property, the land south of which you intend to take for the purposes of your park. I have been unable to lay out a drive along this escarpment which is entirely satisfactory, without encroaching at some points still further on the Merici property. In order to keep south of the line as now proposed the drive would join the Wolfe's Cove road just where the grade is very had, and in addition a sharp curve is required. If a small additional piece of the Merici property is taken the drive can be located as shown oil the accompanying plan, so that it will form practically a continuation of Gilmore Hill road and escape the greater part of this bad grade. I would, therefore, suggest that the taking the line through the Merici property he changpd as shown on the accompanying plan.
If there is anything in this report or on the plans which I have not made clear, about which you wish additional information, kindly let me know.
Respectfully submitted,
(Sgd.) FREDERICK G. TODD.
Is this money that is put at the disposal of the commission in the hands of the Receiver General or in the hands of the commission?
In the hands of the commission.
How does it come then that parliament is asked to grant power to the commission to spend their own money?

At the time the commission was created it was provided that not a red cent of the money received from the various parts of the empire should be spent without receiving the sanction of the Dominion parliament, and also of the Governor in Council. With this sanction, the people of the country will have confidence that their money is being properly expended.

Even with the consent of the Governor in Council, if parliament has a right to give authority to use this money for that purpose, it comes under the control of the Crown in such a way as to require the consent of the Governor in Council. Besides that we are either taking or purchasing a highway that, I presume,

will be for all time in the future a charge upon the revenue; it will have to be kept up by the government.
We do not buy it ourselves.

Though it should come to us by wav of gift, we still will be charged with the responsibility of maintaining it tor all time. In addition to that, parliament will likely be invited to give an additional amount to that commission to carry out the purposes which they have in view. I think it would be well to take a little time to consider it.
the commission to make a loan to the to*vn of $15,000, without interest for a certain length of time, after which interest will be paid at the rate of three per cent.
I am very doubtful of the right of parliament to sanction anything of that kind; I do not think it was ever contemplated when this trust was created that an adventure of this kind should be entered upon. If the municipality of Montcalm feels disposed to make a gift let them do so, but for us to authorize a loan by this trust would not be a proper thing. Was not a considerable portion of the money now in hand contributed by the Dominion parliament?

I have stated that the moneys belong to the commission. The commission was appointed by parliament, and it was resolved then that_ nothing should be spent towards the acquisition of land or property except it were done under the supervision of the Dominion government. This being a national park, it is well that parliament should have control over the enterprise.

Will not this money have to be paid out of the consolidated revenue, and will it not be a charge upon the consolidated revenue, if they commence the undertaking now and acquire property that must of necessity compel them to pay out money in the future?

There is no question but that later on, if the commission comes to parliament to get some further aid towards beautifying or maintaining this park, then such aid will have to be introduced by way of resolution. But in the present case the object is to give legislative sanction to an act of the commission, an act to purchase property with their own funds which they Bold in trust.
Does the proposed purchase include the Ross Rifle factory?

No.
Mr. LENNOX- There are a few points which the minister has not explained fully. First, I would like to know why this matter has been delayed until now. In common with many other members, I _ have very serious objection to matters being rushed through the House when we have not proper time to consider them, and I do not think we have proper time to consider this matter now. I would like to know in the second place what is the urgency for doing it now. Then I would like to know as to the acreage of land it is proposed to acquire, and what is the amount of expense contemplated. I would like a fuller explanation as to the proposal of the town of Montcalm. I understood the minister to say that Montcalm proposed to make a gift, and that in consideration of that gift he wishes to authorize

I shall be glad to state the amount in the hands of the commission on the second or third reading of the Bill. I gather from the hon. member for St. Lawrence division, Montreal (Mr. Bick-erdike), who is a member of the commission, that they have about $300,000 in cash, perhaps a little more.
I want to know if any came from the Dominion government?

Certainly. The laTge portion of that amount came from the various provinces of Canada, but a very large amount from other sections of the empire. As regards the proposed arrangement with the town of Montcalm, I shall read a letter which I have received from Sir George Garneau, president of the commission, who
says:
As to the proposed loan of a sum not exceeding $15,000 to the town of Montcalm, the position is as follows:
It was at first intended to connect the two battlefields, of the Plains of Abraham and of Ste. Foy, by widening the present Belvidere road and making it one of the Park avenues and authority to acquire the necessary land on the east side of the Belvidere road for the purpose of widening was granted by 7-8 Edward VII, chapter 58, schedule No. 6. The acquiring of this land would have cost over $19,000. The commissioners now propose to open a new avenue instead of utilizing the Belvidere road, which new avenue will be in line with the Ste. Foy monument and will greatly improve the general scheme of the park. The municipality of the town of Montcalm has agreed to give to the commission the land required for the proposed avenue on condition that the avenue be built and maintained, as a part of the National Battlefields Park, by the commission. As his municipality is called upon at present o make heavy disbursement on capital account for the laying of water and drainage pipes in the rapidly extending parts of the town, which practically absorbs its borrowing powers, the commission has agreed to advance the amount required for the purchase of the right of way from the private holders on the condition that the municipality cede it to the commission and reimburse the amount by annual instalments extending over thirty years with interest at

the rate of 3 per cent, subject to the approval of parliament. This is the power that is prayed for by article 3 of the proposed Bill. The net result as far as the commission (and the public) is concerned is that instead of paying over $19,000 for the land required to widen the Belvddere road it will get the land for the new avenue gratuitously and build and maintain the avenue in either case.
So it is, in my judgment, a good transaction which is being made by the commission. A few days ago I met two of the commissioners, Mr. Denison of Toronto and Sir Edmund Byron Walker. Sir Edmund Walker stated to the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and myself that he considered this a great improvement on the first scheme to widen the Belvidere road, because it is in a straight line between the Ste. Foye monument and the Plains of Abraham. I do not think any exception should be taken because the commission take the proper precaution of coming before parliament to get the necessary sanction.
What about the urgency?

The tercentenary of Quebec took place in 1908. We are now in 1911. This is the remaining portion of the lands necessary to begin the beautifying, and embellishment of the park. The commission have engaged Mr. Todd, the landscape architect, on the suggestion of the Dominion government, and he has made a very lengthy report which my hon. friend will read in * Hansard ' to-morrow. The people who have subscribed for the acquisition and beautifying of the battlefields naturally wish to know what has been done with their money, and it Is time to start vigorously in order that the work may be accomplished without undue loss of time.
The government knew this three months ago.
This has been before me for some time. The Prime Minister had to introduce the Bill at some time during the session, and I do not think any time has been lost.
It is six months to-day since the House met.
There is nothing in this Bill which is controversial.
Does the minister consider that the proposed arrangement with the village of Montcalm comes within the terms of trust created some years ago?

Certainly, and the very reason that the commission applied to parliament for the sanction of their operations is that they can do by this Act of parliament what they cannot do of their own Mr. LENNOX.
authority. Any transaction of the commission whether by way of loan or sale or purchase must come before parliament.
We created a commission for the disbursement of money for specific purposes, and they have no right to go into an extraneous matter. Have they the right to begin to loan money?
Is it not one way of acquiring land?
They might acquire the land by loan or by payment of cash. I will explain on the third reading.
I raise no objection now to the form of procedure, but I shall ask the ruling of Air. Speaker later on.

UNITED STATES TAX ON CANADIAN SHIPPING.
speechtext:
BARNARD (Victoria, B.C.) I call the attention of the government to the following article published in the Victoria * Daily Colonist ' of May 10, 1911:
A Bill aimed at Canadian shipping under which the coasting steamers plying to the United States ports will be called upon to pay a tonnage tax ranging from 10 cents a ton on vessels of the usual coasting type, to 50 cents a ton on steamers from 4,000 to 8,000 tons register has been introduced at Washington. This is one of two Bills introduced and aimed against Canadian and British shipping. The Bill introduced by Mr. Rucker, of Colorado, contains the following clause.
'Every vessel not of the United States that shall arrive direct from her own country, its colony, or possession, in ballast or merchandise produced there, or with passengers in a less portion than one-third of her burden or capacity, for freight or passengers as aforesaid, shall pay a duty on the gross measurement in addition to the regular duty imposed by law, as follows:	On all vessels
not exceeding 2,000 tons, 10 cents per ton: not exceeding 2,400 tons, 25 cents per ton; between 4,000 and 8,000 tons, 50 cents a ton: between 8,000 and 12,000 tons 75 cents a ton; between 12,000 and 16,000 tons, $1 a ton; between 16,000 and 20,000 tons, $1.25 a ton; exceeding 20,000 tons, $1.25 a ton.'
Under this law, if it comes into effect, the local steamers of the Canadian Pacific railway trading to Seattle would have to pay a tonnage tax of 10 cents a ton, which, in the case of the ' Princess Charlotte ' of 1,925 tons register, would be $192.50 per trip, and the ' Princess Victoria ' would be mulcted $43.30 a trip. The steamers plying to Alaskan Mr. GRAHAM.
ports would also suffer from this law. The Blue Funnel liners and the Weir liners would suffer, being called upon to pay 75 cents a ton for they rarely have passengers to the extent of their tonnage. The Japanese liners, by touching at Victoria, would escape under this law, as by making a call at Victoria, they do not go direct from their home country, but the Japanese lines plying to San Francisco from the Orient would suffer.
Another Bill, introduced into the United States senate on April 20 last, by Mr. Gore, provides that, 'on and after July 1st next, all alien immigrants coming to the United States from any foreign country other than an adjacent country shall be required to embark upon a vessel of American register at a seaport of the country of which he is a lawful citizen, or subject, and of which he has been resident for two years.'
Here is another clause of the same Bill: 'Any and all vessels may be entitled to admission to registry in the United States for the purposes of this Act without regard to the place of construction, and without any requirements as to ownership, except that a majority interest of such vessels shall be owned by citizens of the United States.
This means that no immigrants are in future to be allowed to go to the United States through Canadian ports or by Canadian lines. How immigrants can be brought across the Pacific for the United States under this law is hard to see, for there is but one steamer flying the United States flag in the North Pacific ocean trade, the Min" nesota, which makes about five trips a year.
If these measures receive official sanction at Washington, local transportation men are expecting they will be followed up by measures equally prohibitive in Canadian railways doing an international business. A start has already been made by including in the first Act above mentioned a clause exempting from the operation of the interstate commerce commission and the Sherman AntiTrust Act, freight brought to the United States in American ships.
I would like to ask the government if they have any knowledge of the introduction of these Acts, and if it is their intention to make representations to Washington that they would be, if passed, an undue discrimination against British and Canadian ships?

maintopic: UNITED STATES TAX ON CANADIAN SHIPPING.
speechtext: I have no information at present in regard to such Acts; but if there is any truth in the statements published by this paper, I am quite sure that the government will make the necessary representations.

Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to call the attention of the acting Minister of Militia- to some articles which are appearing in some of the western daily papers. The first article is from the Nelson ' Daily News ' of April 20, and is headed: ' Go to Kamloops Camp or Resign; Situation of Officers in 102nd Regiment; Allege Neglect by Department.' The article says:

'Go to Kamloops on June 5 or resign/ exactly represents the situation in Nelson as regards the order which has been issued l>v Colonel Wadmore, D.O.C., to the effect that the 102nd Regiment shall go into camp on that date; and the unanimous decision of the officers of the regiment as far as can be gathered is that the latter is the only step which they can take.
Further on the article says:
Another point over which there is the greatest dissatisfaction is the drill hall. The armoury here was originally built to accommodate but one company. There are now two companies, a Maxim gun section, a stretcher bearer section, a signalling section, a bugle band and all their equipment. Last year a special store room was obtained by the regimental staff, but this, it is claimed, is far too small to accommodate all the equipment which has to be piled in, more or less discriminately, something after the junkshop manner. The regiment contended that the new rooms are needed for the Maxim gun detachment, for the stretcher bearer corps, for the signallers and for armoury purposes for 'C' Company. For over three years efforts have been made to induce the department to make these improvements with the net result that promises have been given and plans approved but nothing more tangible accomplished.
A little further on, under the heading of ' Ludicrous State of Affairs,' the article says:
A ludicrous feature of the neglect with which the regiment is said to be treated, and the general mismanagement at headquarters which is alleged, is that of clothing. It was learned during the past few days that if the regiment turned out to-morrow some of the men would be without coats, others would be without trousers, and others would be without caps. An instance of this mismanagement is that in 1907 the officers of the regiment were told that they were entitled in 1908 to 2i great coats, while none of these promised coats have arrived so far.
But that was a minor matter compared with the trouble that commenced after the general order was issued in September, 1909, that the green uniforms which up to that time were worn by the Canadian militia, were cancellerl and that they were to be replaced by khaki clothing.
After several months of patient waiting on the part of the local officers, the clothing began to come along from headquarters in driblets, usually in very small and mixed driblets. For instance, one consignment consisted of four caps, eighteen pairs of trousers and five frocks. This varied assortment, naturally, was just sufficient to furnish four men, though one other might have gone on parade nicely dressed but with a bare head, while It others would have made a fine soldierly picture in their undershirts, caps and trousers and without any frocks.
Then, a paper of May 11, just to hand, represents that the dissatisfaction with this state of affairs has reached the climax. Above the article is a picture of Sir Frede-292
rick Borden, and it has these headings: ' Headquarters Officers Hand in Resignations; Officers of Other Units of Regiment Expected to Follow Suit; Ottawa Stands by District Officer Commanding.' Then it goes on to say:
The commissioned officers of the 102nd
regiment R. M. R., in Nelson, which means all the officers of the headquarters establishment comprising 'B' and 'C' companies, Maxim gun section, stretcher bearer section, signalling section, and regimental staff, are resigning as a body, as a protest against the refusal of the Militia Department to pay the regiment for the drill and training of 1910-11. Many of the officers handed in their resignations yesterday, for transmission to the proper quarter, and it is undertsood that the balance will hand them in to-day. The drill and training of 1910-11 was duly performed, both by the headquarters establishment and by the companies in the other towns, but Colonel AVadmore, the new district officer commanding, both refused to grant the inspection requested and refused to allow pay. AVhile this is not the chief ground on which nearly all units in the regiment have refused to attend the annual drill and training ordered for Kamloops in June, it is one oi the grounds, and it is one of the sorest points with the 102nd.
There are reasons for believing that the officers of the companies at Rossland, Kaslo, Revelstoke and Kamloops are about to resign also, on the same ground that serves the officers of the headquarters establishment.
The article then gives a list of the officers. At the time of the trouble in South Africa, no regiment was more prompt in offering its services than this regiment, and no men did better service than the men from these western contingents, and they seem to have a very just ground of complaint.
The hon. gentleman cannot discuss the matter on the orders of the day.
I merely wish to ask what action the denartment intends to take with regard to the resignation of these officers?
If the hon. gentleman will let me have the clippings which he has read, I will inquire in the department and endeavour to get the information.

Yesterday the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. White) asked a question in regard to the military buildings at the Petawawa camp, which had . been destroyed by fire. For his information I beg to say that the buildings were destroyed on the 11th instant. Two buildings at Petawawa camp grounds, the supply and ordnance buildings, were burnt, the fire having originated from lightning. The fire occurred about five o'clock in the



morning, and notwithstanding the fact that within a very short time two streams of water were playing on the buildings, they and their contents were completely burnt, there being a very high wipd blowing at the time. The loss by this fire is approximately as follows: Buildings, $6,000; stores $9,000; a total of $15,000. It is the intention of the department to rebuild these buildings, at least one of them, at once, and probably both.
Was there any insurance?
The memorandum does not say.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday night, in answer to a question of the hon. leader of the opposition, the hon. Minister of Agriculture said that he had cabled to England and expected to get a report with regard to the withdrawal of the Battle of Chateauguay from the Pageant of the Festival of the Empire. I notice in this morning's paper the following press dispatch:
London, May 16.-Frank Lascelles, master of the Festival of the Empire pageant, in an interview to-day with reference to the strictures in the Canadian parliament because of the omission of the Battle of Chateauguay, said it was a storm in a teacup. The abandonment of the scene, he asserted was not due to fear of American feeling, but the result of the conclusion reached by the Canadian committee that the episode was not typical of Canadian life.
I might say that the day before yesterday I received the following letter on this subject:
St. James Street, S. W.
Royal Societies Club,
5th May, 1911.
My dear Sir,-As the author of the scene 'Chateauguay' which was to have been presented at the Festival of the Empire Pageant, I have read your remarks as I find them reported by cable in the 'Times' with very great interest.
At the same time, I should be extremely obliged to you if you would take some occasion to make it publicly known that Lord Strathcona was no party to the suppression of this most picturesque scene.
Several Canadians on the committee feared that the scene, in which a number of American soldiers were to have been represented, might be exaggerated by the Yellow Press of both countries and thereby cause ill feeling most undesirable in connection with such a Festival. For that reason we withdraw it.
Believe me, dear sir,
Faithfully yours, BECKLES WILLSON.
I make no comment except to add that I thoroughly sympathize with the views Mr. KING.
expressed by the leader of the oposition, and can only regret the withdrawal of a feature which should have roused no resentment on anybody's part.
