Before the orders of the day are called I would like to ask the attention of the acting Minister of Marine (Mr. Lemieux) to a letter I have received from a resident in my riding, complaining about a dam built at a place called Galetta on the Mississippi, which destroys the fishing. The letter is as follows:
Almonte, May 9, 1911.
Dear Sir,-Excuse my liberty to ask would you kindly have fishways looked into and provided from the mouth of the Mississippi river to at least Carleton Place lake you could not provide a much greater blessing for the people of the surrounding country.
I may say that the dam complained of is built near the mouth of the Mississippi river which empties into the Ottawa river about a mile or two from where this dam is located, and it is utterly impossible for fish to come out of the Ottawa and up the Mississippi on account of that dam. That dam is built for power purposes, and for supplying light to the town of Arnprior, and is situated about four miles from the village of Galetta. If the hon. minister will look into that, he will confer a great favour on a large number of people who have the pleasure of living along the Mississippi river.

I understand from my hon. friend (Mr. Thoburn) that the people are willing to have the dam, but now they want to have it tempered by a blessing. While it might be in my power to give a dam, I am not quite so sure that I could give the desired blessing.

Mr. TAYLOR (Leeds)-. Might I ask the Postmaster General whether the report, which comes to me on reliable authority, that copies of speeches of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are being sent out in bundles to post offices, and the postmasters are instructed to distribute them, is well founded. I put this question the other day and would like to have a reply.
Unfortunately I was at a funeral yesterday and did not hear the question.
It was put on Monday.
No such instructions are given postmasters. Hon. members on both sides can send out literature, but the postmasters have no right to distribute it.
But if they are doing it?
Then they are acting contrary to instruction.
If it he proved that they are doing it, will the Postmaster dismiss them?

I would certainly warn any postmaster who did anything of the kind. Some of them may have done it through ignorance. I warn them publicly now that they have no right to distribute for anybody literature sent to them.
Was it due to ignorance on the part of the gentlemen who sent out the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister?
It may have been due to ignorance on the part of some postmasters, but they have their instructions and ought to know their duty.

Would the publisher of a newspaper such as the Toronto 'Globe' have the right to send bundles of that paper to country postmasters and have them placed in the post office boxes without being addressed?

That is quite different. A postmaster may receive a list of subscribers from the proprietor of a newspaper and distribute the newspapers according to that list. Some times there is no time to address the newspapers and they are sent in bundles so as to catch the early train, but the usual way is to label each newspaper.

Can the publisher of a newspaper send a hundred copies to a country postmaster to be distributed by him to people who are not subscribers?
292}
No.

That was done in the general elections, I think. It was done in my own town with the Toronto 'Globe,' and that is why I asked the question. I understand the Postmaster General to say that no newspaper can send a bundle to a country postmaster to be circulated to people who are not subscribers?

That is against the post office regulations. They can only be sent to bona fide subscribers who have paid their subscriptions, and are entered on the list. No postmaster is allowed to distribute bundles of newspapers which are not regularly subscribed for.
Suppose they call it a sample copy.

A sample copy is allowed, but there are rules governing sample copies. No one has the right to send a bundle of papers to a postmaster to be distributed to people who are not subscribers. The postmaster must be given a bona fide subscription list, otherwise he is not allowed to distribute the newspapers and the proprietor is liable under the law.
It might be well for the hon. minister to issue a circular to his postmasters notifying them to that effect.
My hon. friend will find that in black and white in the Post Office guide.
But the minister might send a little reminder to the public.
I give that reminder now, that it is done.

Is there any regulation by which a newspaper publisher has the Tight to send a list of his subscribers, and then send a bundle of newspapers not individually addressed, and have the postmaster open that bundle and distribute the newspapers according to the list?
No. That is against the regulations.

I would like to ask another question. The Postmaster General intimated a few moments ago that he knows that this is sometimes done, but not very generally. Does not the minister think it his duty to see that it is not done?
Certainly.
Will he do it?

It is not a criminal offence. Take a case in point. Suppose the Ottawa ' Citizen ' or the Ottawa ' Free Press,' wishes to serve a place, and to serve it must catch a particular train. When the time comes to

catch that train, they have only 200 or 300 papers printed. I asked the hon. member (Mr. Lennox), would it be human in me to prosecute the ' Citizen ' for that when it is done in good faith. This is a regulation for the protection of the department and public, but it must be administered in good faith.
The hon. minister asked me a question, I would like to answer it.
I am afraid I cannot allow the debate
The minister asks a question.
But there must be a stop put to it somewhere.
May I not answer the question?
It is against the rules to continue
As I put the question I would like the hon. gentleman to have an opportunity to answer it.
The only difficulty is that if I grant permission to one member I cannot refuse it to others.
Very well, I will take it up later.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 211) to grant certain aid towards construction of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company-Mr. Graham.
On section 1,
1. His Majesty, on behalf of the Dominion of Canada (hereinafter called 'the Government') may aid and assist the construction and completion by the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company (hereinafter called 'the Company') of a line of railway extending from the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, to the city of Port Arthur, in the province of Ontario, including the mileage of the line (lying between the said points) 'already in part constructed by the company and by the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company extending from a point in the province of Quebec opposite the town of Hawkes-bury to Rideau Junction, west of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, and including the line already constructed by the company extending from a point in the township of Cap-reol, in the province of Ontario, to or near Sellwood Junction, by guaranteeing the principal and interest of -the bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities (hereinafter called 'the guaranteed securities') of the company, to the extent of thirty-five thousand dollars per mile of the said line of railway so aided, which guaranteed securities to the extent aforesaid, the company is here-Mr. LEMIEUX.
by authorized to create and issue; interest on the guaranteed securities to be at the rate of three and one-half per cent per annum, payable half yearly; the principal to be payable in fifty years from the passing of this Act. The government may, subject to the provisions of this Act, enter into a contract with the company fixing the terms and conditions upon which the guarantee is given and of the security to be taken therefor.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The minister (Mr. Graham), stated that the route would be given more definitely in the Bill than in the resolution. But that is not the case.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I did say to my hon. friend that I thought perhaps it would be more definitely stated. But, in looking over it, I do not see how we can state it more definitely. The route has to be approved by the Railway Department with final approval by the Railway Commission. I gave the route in a general way, and it cannot vary very far from the line I mentioned the other day, and as given in the resolution.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That, I suppose, is more or less a formal matter. You never find the Railway Commission varying very much from the general line of the route proposed.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: About a mile perhaps- they cannot vary very much.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Therefore, there does not seem to be very much ground in that contention. This is rather important because the preamble of the Bill declares that among other objects this railway is for the purpose of opening up, and developing portions of the country as yet without railway facilities. The Bill states one terminus as being in Port Arthur and the other in Montreal. Rideau Junction is named, and also a line of railway partly constructed. But otherwise the route seems to be entirely indefinite as between Port Arthur, on the west, and Monteral on the east. If the object is to open up and develop the country now without railway facilities, one would suppose that the route would be stated, and that looking at the Bill we could see that the preamble is carried out by the terms of the' enactment.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The route, as I stated it the other day, is as definite as it could be made until we come to actual location. The charter _ of the company states where they can build. Beginning at Port Arthur, as I outlined the other day, that part

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
The minister need not go over that again. When we come to deal with the realities of the situation, the company will be bound by the Bill, and not by the minister's speech.

Therefore, his explanation does not put us very much further along. My point is that there should be something in the Bill binding the company as to the route, since the alleged purpose is to give railway facilities to portions of the country that are not yet provided therewith.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: To fix the route in the Bill would mean, that, if there were engineering difficulties the road could not be built. As a matter of fact the route of this road has to be approved by the Railway Department before the company can start construction, the final location has-to be approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not see how we can describe it more particularly in the Bill.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
I understand you cannot point to a single county in Ontario through which the road must run, according to the terms of the Bill.
to pass this Bill until the location is better defined. The Railway Commission can deviate, but they must have something ter deviate from, and there is nothing in thff Bill to guide them. I would not tie the company to an exact location within a mile or so, but we certainly should say it should pass through certain named parishes, townships or counties.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: In the old settled country it is easy to do that, but this line will run through territory that has never been opened up, and it is difficult to describe it. You might put something in the Bill that .would prevent the building of the road at all if it "were restricted in that way, when you come to approve of the route map. There has to be some discretion left to the department in approving of a particular route through such territory, else you may defeat the object we have in mind.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I presume there is nothing in the statute which says they must rur to certain points except that they must gr to Ottawa, Hawkesbury, Carillon, Montreal and Port Arthur. The department will certainly locate the line along the most feasible and practicable route. The company intends to run through Renfrew, Nipissing, and all through that country to within sixty miles of Port Arthur, when they get closer to the Canadian Pacific railway.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: How near does the road approach the other lines if that intention is carried out?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific railway skirts the Ottawa river, and this road will cross the Ottawa into the province of Quebec, and will return in the locality of Portage du Fort, and then it will go to the town of Beachburg. There are points where it will be 10 miles from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and other points where it will be 40 or 50 miles away. On the way to Pembroke it will go through territory not touched by the Canadian Pacific Railway.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The Railway Committee would not grant a charter for such an indefinite location as this.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: They have a charter.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Why should not this company, which is heavily subsidized by the people, define more particularly the route, as indicated by the Minister of Railways in his remarks?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Even the minister cannot deviate from the charter of the company.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: We should not involve the credit of the country in helping a railway, the location of which is * so indefinite. I do not think we should be asked

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: This line is about 1,000 miles long, between Montreal and Port Arthur, and whilst some of that territory is new, its physical features are fairly well known. We inferred from what the minister said that there have been explorations sufficient to enable the company to know pretty well the cost per mile of building this line, and there appears to be sufficient data to move the government to give a guarafltee of $35,000 per mile. The minister should at least have defined in this Act certain points through which it will pass, so that we may know that we are promoting the building of a railway through a country which it is desirable to open up.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Let the clause stand and we will see if it can be better defined.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Is there anything in the Bill which fixes the outside mileage that we guarantee? Are we sure that the road will not be 1,500 miles instead of 1,000?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There is a clause in the Bill which says that the decision of the Governor in Council as to the mileage shall be absolute.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That is only as to the measurement.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It does not say so.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It certainly means that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Possibly it does. However, the approximate distance is one thousand miles and the department would not be so negligent as to let them build all around the country.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There should be a limit in the Bill saying ' not exceeding ' a certain distance.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It is rather unusual to ask a guarantee at the rate of so much per mile for an indefinite mileage.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
You should say not
exceeding so many miles.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It would be easy enough to do that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It is rumoured that instead of being 1,000 miles it was 1,200 miles.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I have never heard of that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
There is a lot of information on this side of the House that you never heard of.
On section 2,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: How is the security that the government takes to be paid out to the railway company?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The proceeds of the sales of the guaranteed stock are placed to the credit of the government and are paid out from time to time upon the certificate of the government engineers.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That would mean a thorough survey by the government as to the quantities taken out and the estimates. If you fix the price the parties are to get for the material removed you can pay out as the work proceeds, but unless all that is provided for I do not see how you can guard yourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The guarantee being for so much per mile, all that would be necessary to see to would be that that amount of money was expended on fair and reasonable terms on the mileage as respects which the certificate is given. We have nothing specifically to do with the terms of the contracts, but if the prices were excessive or unreasonable or did not represent a bona fide expenditure, the government engineer would certainly not certify them. I think that is the- only check we have. The contracts made between the company and the contractors are not matters directly under our control.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
The danger is this:	Suppose a construction company is
formed by the same parties who own the railway; the railway company enters into an arrangement with the construction company, as nearly every railway company does, for the purpose of getting this road constructed. The prices may be fancy prices. The security of the government may amount to double the actual cost of the work. The amount paid goes into fhe hands of the construction company. The necessity then arises for the government to have an exact valuation of the work done and Mr. LENNOX.
the exact quantities, and to pay out the money on these securities just as they would pay out cash on a contract of their own.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The government do not pay out securities at all. The securities are sold in the market, and the proceeds are placed to the credit of the government, and are then paid out from time to time on the certificate of the government engineer.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Does the government exercise any supervision over the payments to contractors? Does it see that the contractors have been paid before it releases the money?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There is a clause in the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company providing that the material that goes into the road must be paid for. Cases have arisen in which sub-eontraetoTs have run bills for materials that did not go into the road, and the government engineers have held up the money until an attempt has been made to have a settlement of these bills. Some of them have been found collectable under the contract and others not.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Suppose that contractors either for work or for material had a lien on the road for a large amount of money that was1 owing to them, it would be necessary that the government should take note of all that in releasing this money.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I think that would be a part of the agreement with the company. If we are paying public money or going security, we ought to know that there would be no lien prior to the government security.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
That should apply not only to the contractors, but to the workmen. The contractors might get the money and not pay the men.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.
On section 3,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: In the case of a contractor or subcontractor who has not paid for material or labour, and where a lien is filed against the railway, what precaution is taken to see that the lien is discharged?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I am informed that workmen cannot enforce a lien against a railway. We proteot, however all these interests in our guarantee contract just as we do in our subsidy contract. We insert a clause providing that if claims are made against any of the contractors for material or labour, these must be paid or we retain a certain amount until they are settled.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That applies to subcontractors as well?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Yes, it applies to all the labour and material that goes into the work.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: You are only mortgaging the bonds, and I would assume that the company sells the bonds and realizes the money.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Then the money is in the hands of the company.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: No, the bonds are sold and the money is deposited with the Receiver General, and is released from time to time as the work progresses on the certificate of the engineer in the Railway Department.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There are two matters which should be had in mind. One is that the proceeds of the bonds guaranteed shall be applied to the purpose for which the guarantee was given. These proceeds, I understand, are taken charge of by the Finance Department, and the department pays out the money according to the amount of work performed, upon the report of its own engineer, reserving a certain amount to meet any contingency.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The other thing necessary is to insure that subcontractors, and contractors under them, and the men employed shall be paid, and that no contractor shall retain money which ought to be paid out for material and work. From what the Minister of Finance has said, I take it that that point is pretty well covered, though I am not quite sure.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: We make a contract with the company as to this guarantee, and we put in that contract a section which protects the working men and those who supply material either to contractors or subcontractors, and the department reserves the right to retain funds until these demands are settled.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I understand from the Minister of Finance that his department takes precautions to the end that these moneys shall be applied only to the purposes for which the guarantee is granted.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That is ascertained by the examination and report of the engineer of the Railway Department?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
Quite so.
On section 10,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Does the government hold all this money until work is commenced, and then pay it out according to the work being done?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
As the Finance Minister explained a few moments ago, the bonds are disposed of and the money is deposited with the Receiver General and paid out as the work proceeds, on the certificate of the engineer, and the auditing of the books by the auditor.
On section 13,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What is the penalty?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
As I said the other night, I am still of the same opinion, that we have done the utmost that can be done in order to encourage trade through Canadian ports. I do not think that any penalty you can place there will help the situation in the least.
On section 14,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I move that after the words ' Port Arthur ' we insert the words ' Ottawa.' That will give us three chief terminals.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Why do you put that in the disjunctive? You say that the company is bound to consent to an order providing for use by the government or by such other railway company ' of the terminals at Port Arthur -or Montreal.' It is meant to include both, is it not?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: We will say * Port Arthur, Ottawa and Montreal, or either.'

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What are the terminals used for the Intercolonial in Montreal? If I remember rightly, there is a joint ownership between the Grand Trunk railway and the Intercolonial, and the expenses are paid according to the user. Who are the owners of the terminals?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The terminals are owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We have a rental arrangement by which we use their lines from Ste. Rosalie to Montreal, and also their terminals. For that we pay $140,000 odd a year. In addition to that we have a traffic arrangement with certain conditions as to the upkeep of the road, and of the terminals.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Do we not get the ownership in some manner, or was that in connection with the bridge, that by a contribution we acquired a joint ownership with the Grand Trunk?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
The proposed arrangement is not with the Grand Trunk. The Canadian Northern will probably have terminals there, and, as I suggested the other night, the time may come when we will wish to compel the Canadian Northern to connect with the Intercolonial railway, to

hand us its traffic, but it will probably not be through the Grand Trunk terminals.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
The object of the section is to provide that- if the government, through the default of the company, is obliged to buy in the railway or any part of the railway from Montreal to Port Arthur, it shall also be in a position to acquire the terminals, since otherwise they could not operate the road. This is a paragraph which was put in at my own suggestion after we had discussed the resolution. We were told in very eloquent terms of the great advantage to the country of our obtaining a lease for certain purposes of the Grand Trunk terminals at Montreal. One is never impressed in visiting the terminals there, with the idea that the Intercolonial railway is very much to the fore; it is very difficult to find the headquarters or location of Intercolonial railway at these terminals. I have had occasion sometimes to look it up, and I find it housed in a little cock-loft upstairs, a very absurd looking place and altogether out of keeping with the character of a road which covers 1,600 or 1,700 miles of territory. If one wants very much information about the operations of the Intercolonial railway, it is not always the easiest thing to get it there, it is much easier to get it here.
This agreement looks forward to an interchange of traffic between the Intercolonial railway and this road. How will it be possible to bring that about? We have our terminals in Montreal fixed for the next 90 years. I suppose it might be possible to interchange traffic between the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial railway in Montreal, even if the terminals were at a considerable distance apart, but I would like to understand what the situation will be. How will this interchange of traffic be arranged? The idea in 1898, and 1899, when this country bought the Drummond County railway and leased a portion of the Grand Trunk railway as well as the terminate, the idea then was to make our traffic arrangements, or, as the minister very graphically expressed it, to hook up, with the Grand Trunk railway. Now, apparently, we are looking forward to the project of unhooking from the Grand Trunk railway and hooking up with the Canadian Northern railway. That will not be quite so simple an operation as it would appear on its face, if I am correct in my appreciations of the conditions, but I do not understand enough about it to be able to form a correct judgment. For that reason, I would like the minister to explain what will 'be the outcome in that respect.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is ah-solutely correct as to its not being a very Mr. GRAHAM.
simple proposition. If it had been quite simple perhaps we would have gone further in this Bill and outlined an agreement about to be made, but the situation with the Grand Trunk railway is as described by my hon. friend. We have a lease with them for 99 years. We have a traffic arrangement' with them for the interchange c! traffic at Montreal which the government can break by giving notice but which the company has no right to end of its own motion.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: You cannot breaK the lease of the terminals?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: No, it is the traffic arrangement. The Grand Trunk railway are already urging very strongly and so are the Grand Trunk Pacific, their interests being identical, that the traffic arrangement may be brought to a close. We could not afford at present to bring the traffic arrangement to a close because if we did the need for using the terminals at Montreal would be largely diminished as our traffic would be reduced to the extent of $1,500,000 each year. But the Grand Trunk Pacific being constructed down to the eastei'n provinces, and the interests of the Grand Trunk railway being identical with theirs, they are already beginning to feel their way to see if some arrangement could not be arrived at by which they could be relieved from the obligation to give us their traffic.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Do they carry out the arrangement?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
They do pretty thoroughly now. There were differences of opinion when the arrangement was first made. A board of arbitrators settled a number of matters such as Montreal being the junction point instead of some other place. It will undoubtedly be strongly urged in years to come that from Levis at least the Grand Trunk Pacific should be allowed to carry the traffic. We are not in a position now to release the Grand Trunk railway from this contract, but it may be in the interest of the public, it will certainly be in the interest of the through Transcontinental line, and it may be in our own interest that that arrangement should be broken if at the same time we could make other satisfactory arrangements. We would prefer to have our terminal arrangements part of the agreement to enter into a traffic arrangement, and I think it is in the interest of the Intercolonial railway that we should be in a position to go to the Canadian Northern, and make a proposition to them that they should enter into an arrangemlent with us to interchange traffic, both through and local, as the Grand Trunk railway is doing with its local traffic. That is why I was careful to put it in that way. We are

taking the power to say to the Canadian Northern railway when we are ready to- do that:	You must enter into such an arrangement with us. But we could not say that now, because we are not in a position to enter into an arrangement.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What did the Minister of Public Works mean the other night by stating that we could only break that agreement with the Grand Trunk railway by serious loss to the government?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What I said was that if parliament now were to make it obligatory on the part of the Minister of Railways to cancel the agreement with the Grand Trunk railway, that company would know that the Minister of Railways was bound by the Act of parliament to cancel the agreement, and, therefore, they would be in a position to exact terms which might be very detrimental to the Intercolonial railway and might inflict a loss upon that railway which would not be likely to be sustained if the Minister of Railways were allowed a free hand to deal with the Grand Trunk in the matter.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: This is the last clause of the Bill, and I would avail myself of the opportunity, before the Bill goes out of committee, to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) if it is intended to push this important measure through before the adjournment^

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I hope so.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Is it intended that the Bill shall go through before the adjournment?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I have that in my mind. I am very anxious to get it through this House, so that it may go to the Senate.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I have listened to the discussion while the Bill was in the committee, and I must say that although that discussion has gone largely upon details, it has left a number of questions which appear to me to be unanswered. Furthermore, it seems to me that for the consideration of a Bill such as this the House would require more time. It is a measure, of the very greatest importance. I believe that very - few of the members of this House are informed as to the details of the measure. We have not had time. Yet it is being rushed through. Is that wise? We are undertaking to fasten on the public a liability of $35,000,000-that is, if the calculation of the distance over which the guarantee extends is one thousand miles. But there is not a man in this House wha can say whether that is the exact distance or not. It more probably is twelve huhdred miles, in which case we are pledging the credit of the country for $42,000,000.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) will permit me-I have an amendment to suggest that the Bill provide that it shall not exceed 1,050 miles.,

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
That may be the information of my hon. friend (Mr. Graham). I have heard that the distance is greater than that. But it has not been measured. But my hon. friend will admit that even at 1,050 miles, the liability is very large. Yet we really have not had opportunity to consider the measure. There are a number of clauses in the Bill itself which seem to go into details as, for instance, clause 14, which we have put through in a very few minutes, but the experience we liaye is that these clauses are nothing but a screen. They may be eluded, they have been eluded in the past, and will be in the future; there is no doubt about that. I consider that, under these circumstances, when the House is on the eve of adjourning through necessity for a few weeks

1 am using a strong expression, but not too strong it seems to merits a public scandal, nothing less, to push through a measure of this importance. No man in the House has had any opportunity whatever to go fully into the question and get all the information which we ought to have. I say this

the public cannot be aware of such undue haste, or we should all be condemned for rushing through an agreement of such magnitude under such circumstances of levity. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that there is no reason. Hon. gentlemen are aware that-probably through our own fault but also largely through the fault of the government-measures of this kind are brought in at the end of every session; they are rushed through, and we have no time to look into them. It is not right; it is not fair to our constituents; it is an injustice to the country. For my part, I wish to enter a protest against the passage of this Bill.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Of course, if we were discussing this matter for the first time-I presume my hon. friend was not here when this Bill was discussed on the resolutions, some-days ago. We took a whole day for a full discussion, and did not rush it. The Bill is exactly as the resolutions were, with some .very slight amendments which we think a little improves them.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) calls that a full discussion. Members get up who face these resolutions for the first time, and ask questions. I do not think I am doing injustice to the minister when I say that, generally, he cannot get positive and categorical answers. You cannot in half a day discuss any transaction of over $30,000,000. In such a time you cannot get a satisfactory discussion of a measure of that kind. The matter would have to be gone into in the minutest detail as such matters are in other countries. I venture to say there is not a legislature in the world

mi
that puts through measures of this kind with such speed. As a matter of fact, I am perfectly sure that we could take up these clauses, examine them carefully and find a multitude of unanswered queries which would suggest themselves at once to our minds. I can only protest, but I think it my duty to do so.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: To utilize the terminals at Montreal, you will have to have an exchange with the Intercolonial at the Grand Trunk station. I do not see how you can do it otherwise. My recollection is that we have a half ownership in the terminals at the Grand Trunk at the city of Montreal. That was given to us in exchange for our assistance in the widening of the bridge going into Montreal. We pay a lease to them of $140,000, and we have joint ownership of the terminals.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I think we have not joint ownership of the terminals.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What sanction is provided in case of the non-execution of this clause 14? Without going into the subsections this provides for an agreement to secure suitable terminals in Montreal. This is like the preceding section where there is no sanction whatever provided in regard to the route-and we know what the clauses about routing traffic amount to ; they do not amount to a row of pins- they are violated every day. What is going to happen if the railway company will not enter into, the agreement as regards these terminals in Montreal? And if it declares that it is ready to make an agreement with the government, as foreshadowed- though it is nothing else but foreshadowed- who is going to decide whether the terminals are suitable or not? Is there any independent authority? Will the city of Montreal have anything to say? The whole of that clause 14 is to my mind nothing but a screen.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The establishment of terminals at Montreal or anywhere else can not be undertaken until after an arrangement is made with the city and approved by the Railway Commissioners, or at any rate approved by the Railway Board. The practice in all such large places is to have a thorough discussion of the city's interests in the matter, and then the Railway Commission says what precautions must be taken.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
We have but the dictum of a minister that nothing will be done without these precautions, but seeing that this legislation is bound to be put through in a short space of time, and that the country i3 to he made liable for $35,000,000, talking on my part will not prevent it, Let me ask if there is a report extant from some Mr. MONK.
responsible person as to the advisability and safety of this enormous guarantee.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There is no special report from anybody. The government made full inquiry, and are fully satisfied that security is ample, and that it will not cost the country a cent.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That is the usual answer we get from this government, but I venture to say there is not another legislature in the world that would pass in this way such an important transaction without having before it the report of competent and independent men as to the value of the security offered, and the necessity for giving this guarantee. Sometimes guarantees are necessary and beneficial, and sometimes they are not, excepting to individuals who make money from them. We have no report as to the advantages the country will get from this immense risk it is taking.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways, said that the estimated cost of this railway is from $50,000 to $55,000 per mile, and the guarantee being only $35,000 per mile and being a first charge against the railway, the security was therefore considered ample. I have been told by several people who professed to know-I cannot vouch whether it is a fact or not-that this railway will be constructed, as the Canadian Northern railway have been accustomed to construct their roads, for a total expenditure of not 'more than $35,000 per mile. If that be so the government would be practically building the railway and handing it over to the Canadian Northern. There is a good deal of force in the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Monk) that there should be before parliament some reliable estimate and information. We ought to know what evidence has been laid before the government to satisfy them that the $35,000 per mile liability is really secured. It occurs to me that if there is anything in the statement that the Canadian Northern in the past has been constructing railways and operating them too, through a country just as difficult as this, at a cost of not more than $35,000 per mile, then it is indispensable that the government should have a proper and reliable estimate made, so that we may be sure we are not guaranteeing the full cost of the road. If it should turn out that default is made by the railway company and that the government is forced to foreclose and acquire the railway, it will not be a very good bargain if, after the railroad has been operated long enough for the company to make default, the government has to take it over at its original cost which would be more than the railway was worth at the time of foreclosure.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I do not think any person experienced in railway engineering and knowing the country through _ which this line runs would suggest that it would be built for $35,000 per mile. We have laid down a standard to which they must build and there is no doubt such a railway cannot be built for $35,000 a mile.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The point is that the government asks parliament to authorize a guarantee of bonds to the extent of $35,000 per mile, and bases the application upon the assertion that the road will cost $50,000 per mile; surely that statement ought to be supported by some authoritative report by engineers of standing. Up to the present we have nothing but the more or less casual assertion of the minister that his engineers informed him the road will cost so much.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: It is common talk that the promoters of this railway have been building railways for less money than they were able to sell their bonds and securities upon that railway for, and that they are growing rich day by day by this means, and that this is only another scheme for adding to their accumulation of wealth. In order to put a finality to that sort of talk, if there is nothing in it, it would be in the interests of the railway as well as in the interests of the government that proper inquiry should be made. There is no denying the fact that this is common talk and common belief among the people of the country.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Part of this Tailway in the province of Quebec can certainly be built for less than $35,000 per mile. I assert that because I know the country. I am perfectly certain of what I say. At the figures given by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, we are undertaking for 1,050 miles a liability of thirty-six and three-quarter millions of dollars. The minister has said that he discussed the resolution during an afternoon, and now we are putting the measure through finally. Does anybody in his senses pretend that that is a sufficient investigation-with no documents before us, no report, only a statement of the minister. We are supposed to be business men, and the country expects us to look into questions of this magnitude according to business methods. In this instance the investigation has been altogether insufficient.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
I do not think I would be doing my duty, as representing a rural constituency, that is not in any way interested' in this road directly, if I permitted this Bill to go through the House without entering my protest against it. It is being rushed through too fast altogether. We have had no time to discuss the project or to give it^ proper consideration. In the short discussion that we have had, we have found already that there are mistakes apparently, in the judgment of at least two members of the government themselves. There has been no estimate provided by competent engineers of the cost of this road. I would have thought that one of the first duties of the government was to have had competent engineers go over this road and estimate its cost to the promoters. But without any estimate before us, we jump to the conclusion to guarantee the bonds of this railway for $35,000 a mile, merely taking the word of the promoters that it is to cost more than the government guarantee. I do not think that is just to the people of this country.
I think that as careful an *estimate of the cost of this road should have been made as if it were a road that the government themselves were building. It looks to me .as if the promoters of this road_ would be able, with this guarantee, to build the road, and pocket a very large amount of money on the transaction. I do not believe that we are acting with good business judgment, or as any business corporation would act in a transaction of this kind. One of the features of the agreement is the routing of freight by the Intercolonial; but when we look into that, we find that the arrangement does not amount to anything at all, because when the freight reaches Montreal over the Canadian Northern, the company can route it to an American port, and there is nothing to prevent them doing so. According to the Minister of Public Works, there is in existence an old agreement with the Grand Trunk that almost prohibits us making this arrangement with the Canadian Northern companv. I find on the Order Paper to-day a notice, of a resolution to lease or take over about 12 branch lines of Tailway in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I do not know what the cost of this will be, but it is sure to involve an enormous additional cost to the country. This guarantee to the Canadian Northern amounts to nearly $40,000,000. The whole thing savours of an election campaign, and an enormous election fund, and the country pays the bill. As the representative of an agricultural constituency. I want to protest against rushing this project through without any consideration in the dying days of the session, in order, if there is to he an election this fall, that a huge campaign fund may be provided for the government.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
I find that I was correct in my statement that the government of Canada is half owner of the terminals at Montreal. I 'will read to the hon. Minister of Railways the clause in the Act which confirms my statement. This is from the agreement mad.e on the 1st day of February, 1898:
927i

And, whereas, for the purpose of' carrying out the said extension the said company is willing that, for the conducting of the business and traffic of the Intercolonial railway, Her Majesty shall have an undivided one-half share or leasehold interest in the company's railway and property between and including Ste. Kosalie and St. Lambert station at the eastern end of Victoria bridge, together witli the use of the company's railway and property between and including Ste. Rosalie and Bonaventure station in the city of Montreal, the use of the Victoria bridge across the River St. Lawrence and of the terminals and connections hereinafter more particularly described, together with an undivided one-half interest in and use of the bridge across the Chaudiere river, and of so much of the tracks and line of the said company in connection therewith as are hereinafter described, all of which right, title, property, interest and user shall be used, enjoyed and exercised to the same extent as if the said railway and property were owned by Her Majesty.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: For what length of time?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: For 99 years, the lease is made.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What is the rental?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Nearly $150,000 a year. Besides that, we paid in cash for making an addition to the Ste. Rosalie branch, and for broadening the Victoria bridge. We become half owners of that.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Half owners for a limited time.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: we are only giving security for $35,000 out of the $50,000. That is not the kind of statement which the people are entitled to. We are entitled to all the details of the cost of this undertaking, including the terminals and rolling stock. We ought also to have the route more accurately defined. To give a company the power to build a railway from Ottawa to Port Arthur, without mentioning the objective points, is very dangerous. In the Railway Committee we always insist on certain objective points being mentioned. Why? In order to prevent railway companies from dickering with the municipalities and saying to a municipality : unless you agree to pay us a bonus or give certain other favours, we shall go in another direction. So that we ought to see that the objective points of this railway are specifically mentioned. But the minister says they have a charter. Well, I have not seen the charter, and we do not know where it is. There is no evidence yet before the House as to the charter this company has. We should not leave to the Minister of Railways and the Board of Railway Commissioners the locating of this road. We have the right to knov where it goes. We have the right to know which particular route is to be adopted in the building of this line. As my hon friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says, the information given us is of the most meagre kind ever presented to this House, when asking this House to vote a guarantee to such a large extent.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways said, in answer to a statement of mine, that anybody would know that this railway could not be constructed through certain portions where it was intended to go for anything like $35,000 per mille. While that may be true as regards the north shore of Lake Superior, are there not other portions-for instance, all of the line east of the particular point I have mentioned-where the road could be built for very much less? If I understood the minister rightly before adjournment, he could not say exactly where the line would be located and would not undertake to define in the Bill the exact location. If that be correct, how can he say that it is going to cost $50,000 per mile to construct a railway, when he does not know where it is going to be constructed?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will study the general contour of the country, he will find that it would not mako any difference whether the railway went 10 miles one way or the other. The cost in either case would be practically the same. In the map which I laid on the table, hon. gentlemen will find that there is a route approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners and the Railway Department which this line proposes to take. That route was ap-

proved after full argument before the Railway Commission and the Minister of Railways by every interest involved. All were present and all laid their views before the commissioners and the minister, and a considerable portion of this line has been finally located by the commission. We could not change that again without full notice being given to all the parties.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: What portion from Ottawa to Port Arthur?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: From Sudbury to Port Arthur has been approved by the Railway Commission, after hearing the representatives of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railw.ay, and all others interested. A piece from Montreal to Georgian Bay has been approved by the Minister of Railways. A short portion east of North Bay and through to Sudbury is the only portion that has not been approved after hearing all the parties.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Why could not the route be defined in the Bill?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: For this reason. Supposing when the company came to construction that, for some reason, every interest would see that it ought to be moved, neither the railway commission nor the Minister of Railways nor any one else would have the right to move it. There was the statute, and we could not vary it. But no change can be made in the approved route without all parties interested being heard.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: There is a part, the minister says, from Montreal to ' Pembroke; you go up to the Falls there, cross over and come back again to the Ontario side of Portage du Fort-has that portion been approved?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That has all been approved after every one interested was heard, except a few miles on either side of Pembroke. That was delayed in order to allow the company to go to Pembroke and make some arrangement which would be suitable to that city.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Does the provincial land grant apply to this line?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Then they get not only the provincial land grant but our guarantee as well.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
The minister says all parties.' That reminds me of the story of the judge who asked the lawyer if he had any authorities in support of his proposition, ' Yes,' said the lawyer, 'your honour, all the authorities are in favour of my proposition.' What 'parties' does the minister mean? There is a 'party' for whom we
are acting-the people of Canada. We are their representatives. But we have not had an opportunity of looking into this matter.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That shows distinctly that what I said is correct. My hon. friend knows from his own experience-and I leave it to his own experience-that where his constituency is interested in a line of railway, he is informed of the hearing. And when a town or municipality is affected, the mayor is notified. And so it is with the representative of every parish They are the people who are interested in seeing where the road is to Tun, particularly so far as local interests are concerned.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Who notifies the members of the House as to the hearings?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Where a constituency is interested in the location of the line, it is the duty of the Department of Railways to inform the member for that constituency. And I think it is invariably done. Certainly these are the instructions that have been given. And, in the same way, the mayors of towns are notified. I am sure I never have a hearing on a route map in my department when there are not members of parliament there because of having been notified.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) has asked me as to the route going through Jacques Cartier and neighbouring counties. There is no difficulty about that. But when the route was fixed, there was no question of a guarantee. The point I insist upon is not the route, but the guarantee, the importance and magnitude of the transaction. And when he says-and he has said repeatedly-that 'all parties' have been heard, I can only say that they may have been heard upon the question of the route, and all ques- -tions of that kind, but I say also that we have not had an opportunity to be heard as to this particular transaction, which is being rushed through unfairly.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I was answering an hon. gentleman who was asking me more particularly as to where the railway was going.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: The minister must be mistaken as to these notifications, or he had better give more distinct instructions to his department. Because, in the case of this very railway, the route of which between here and Montreal passes through the county I have the honour to represent, the hearing was held a couple of years ago, and I never had any notification of when the matter was to be brought before the minister. -

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I think it must have been 'longer ago than two years.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I do not know, but it was since I became a member of this House.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I am very careful about that. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) remarked that I did not notify members of the House. I will leave to members about him the refutation of that statement.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: In the case of the Sudbury branch of the Canadian Pacific railway, which was built through my riding since I became a member of this House, 1 got no notice whatever. And I understand there are a good many other members who have had similar experiences. However, that is not the point I wish to speak about. I wish to say a word about the question of the cast of construction. The minister understands that it will cost $50,000 a mile. On the other hand, it is said by hon. members on this side that it cannot cost $35,000 a mile. I am inclined to think, with all deference, that none of us know very much about it. And that is the very difficulty in the matter; we have no more information about this than we had about the Transcontinental. Take the Transcontinental line, say, from Quebec to Winnipeg. We had specific information from the Minister of Finance

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: ' Mountains of information.'

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
Yes, ' mountains of information.' We had not only statements from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) but we had a statement from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) who was advocating the construction of that road. He stated that he had engaged his own engineer to go into the matter, and that this engineer, in conjunction with another engineer who had been over the route, had placed the cost definitely, as an outside figure, at $30,000 a mile for a large portion of this road. There is no reason to believe that that was not stated in good faith, perhaps, but we have the fact now that this railway, 1,800 miles of it -a large portion of it paralleling this 1,000 miles-will cost $100,000 a mile.
An hon-. MEMBER. With stealings.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
Of course, we do not know how much stealings that includes. I do not for a moment imagine that the construction cost anything like $100,000 a mile, if the thing were properly and honestly carried out. But what I am pointing out is that we have a right to some definite information about the cost of construction. But we have the fact that the minister says that he is informed that the total cost will be $50,000 a mile, and then hon. gentlemen on this side state that it Mr. GRAHAM.
cannot be over $35,000 a mile. I venture to say there is no good foundation for the minister's statement. We had an estimate in reference to the Transcontinental that the cost would not exceed $28,000 a mile, including interest, and we know that other estimates put it at from $25,000 up to the estimate of the hon. member for Brandon, $30,000 as an outside figure. And we know also that the cost to the country will be actually $100,000 a mile. Now, we have a right, both on general business principles, and more particularly having regard to the fact that these statements of this government have proved themselves to be utterly unreliable in the past-we have a right, I say, to some definite information about this matter. I am not saying that this road can be built for $30,000 a mile, or that it can be built for $50,000. But what I do say is that as a business proposition we should have placed before us the estimate of engineers who have gone over the route, and who can testify as to the character of the road, and give us a reasonable basis upon which to form an estimate, and that estimate should be laid before the House in advance of our being driven into adopting a measure of this kind. I am entirely in favour of giving reasonable assistance to this company, but I am very much opposed to this system of rushing things in when we are all anxious to go home, and have no reasonable information to justify us in pledging the country to this enormous liability.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
I would remind the minister (Mr. Graham) of the fact that the provincial government of Ontario gave a large land grant to the road that we are asked to furnish $35,000 a mile to build. The hon. gentleman has had considerable experience in politics in the province of Ontario, and if I am not mistaken, he took some part in the last provincial campaign. And the chief argument of the leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackay, in that campaign was that the provincial government had given a land grant to this road far in excess of the value of the road. Any one who heard Mr. Mackay in the Opera House in Ottawa, and his followers throughout the country, knows that that was his argument about this railway. Now, the Dominion government step forward, and give them an additional sum of $35,000 a mile, and do that without giving the matter proper consideration, in the dying hours of the session, without any engineer's report, or any information at all before them in connection with it. We grant this large sum of money, which will amount probably * to nearly $40,000,000. I say it is not right in the public interest that this should be done. We should have had much more time to consider it, and the government

should not rush hastily into this matter. As I said before, it looks very much as if there was something behind this, some reason for it on the part of the government, and I can see no other reason than the fact that a Dominion election is staring them in the face this fall.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: In addition to the land grant, does the provincial government guarantee the bonds too?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
There is a small section of ten miles in the vicinity of Sellwood which comes under the provincial guarantee. That guarantee runs out in twenty years, then ours will become the first mortgage. In the meantime, we get $35,000 a mile of mortgage bonds on another portion of their line to cover that ten miles. Without wanting to drag in political questions, I may say that I think my hon. friend will remember it was that guarantee that Mr. McKay discussed more than the land grant.
Mr. M1DDLEBRO. I notice that one of the principal objects stated in the preamble of the Bill as a justification for the government guaranteeing these bonds, is to afford the government system of railways in Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, an interchange of through traffic. That would also include, I suppose, the proposed branch lines, concerning which there is an item on the Order Paper to-day. Section 14 says:
The company (the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company) and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, respectively, shall enter into an agreement with the government:
(a)	to secure or establish, or cause to be secured or established, suitable terminals for the company within the city of Montreal;
(b)	on the request of the government, to make arrangements with the Intercolonial railway for the interchange of traffic between the company and the Intercolonial railway at Montreal.
I suppose that is one of the chief objects of guaranteeing the bonds. I would like to ask the minister, if the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company refuse either to enter into an agreement, or, having entered into the agreement, refuse to carry out its terms, what remedy has the government against the Canadian Northern Railway Company?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I imagine that if they refuse to enter into the agreement provided under this Act, they would not get the guarantee. It is a part of the Act that they enter into a certain agreement.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: Supposing they agree to do it and do not do it, what remedy has the minister?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That would be a legal point.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: As I understand it, the principal obejct of the agreement is to extend the Intercolonial railway westward?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I think the members on this side of the House understand that one of the chief objects of the agreement is to make the Intercolonial a paying concern by giving it an interchange of traffic with this company. Now they may enter into this agreement, and there is absolutely nothing that I can see to compel them to keep it. All we are doing with the company is to guarantee the bonds. Once we guarantee the bonds, and the company does not carry out the chief object of this agreement, there is, so far as I can see, no remedy. It does not constitute such a default that would justify us in taking possession of the road. They could refuse to carry out the agreement, and we still have to guarantee the bonds. If they make a breach of the object for which we give a guarantee of those bonds, we have no remedy.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I have discussed that point so many times already that perhaps I should not weary the House with repeating it. But I suppose it is a principle of law, or ought to be, that there is a remedy for every wrong. We should discuss the question from a practical standpoint, as well as hanging on the threads of technicalities. Does my hon. friend surmise that they would have a railway all the way from Port Arthur to Montreal and then refuse to have a terminal in Montreal?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: I said my principal objection was that if they refused to enter into an agreement for an interchange of traffic, if, for instance, they should find it more profitable to send their goods by way of Boston or New York than by the Intercolonial, and if they refused to send them by the Intercolonial, you would have no redress, so far as I can see.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: We could proceed against them for damages.

speechtext: What would be the measure of the damages to this government whose only contract is to guarantee ths bonds? You simply have to guarantee their bonds, and you have no measure of damages against this company for not carrying out their agreement.

speechtext: What redress would yon have?

speechtext: If I were making a contract I would make it in such a manner that, if there was a default on the part of the company, I would have some redress. We could seize some portion of their receipts, or something of that kind.

If the actual cost is $55,000 per mile, and we are guaranteeing $35,000, that is a little over 60 per cent. If the cost should be only $30,000, then a guarantee of $20,000 would be sufficient. Then the government's engineer would supervise the construction and you would guarantee a certain percentage of the cost.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: My hon. friend objected to that very principle in the mountain 'sections of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We guaranteed 75 per cent of the cost of construction of the mountain section, but that was not satisfactory. On the prairie section, we put in a maximum amount, a certain percentage not to exceed a certain amount. The railway has cost over $33,000 per mile on the prairie sections, and the guarantee that we gave has not met the expectations of those to whom we gave it. The Grand Trunk Pacific have to raise another loan of $10,000,000. Having the experience of the Grand Trunk Pacific and of the Canadian Pacific railway, from a business standpoint, I believe it is better in the interests of the country to name a stated amount, which would not be decreased and could not be increased and adhere to that amount. I believe this is only a fair proportion of the cost.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext: That may be correct. Surely this estimate of $50,000 a mile must have been founded on something? I would imagine that the minister would not trust to an oral report of an officer of his department, that he would insist on a written report. He must have some information. Why not communicate that to parliament, when his whole case is based on the theory that this road will cost $50,000 per mile? Estimating the cost at $50,000 per mile, we guarantee bonds to the extent of 70 per cent of its cost. That is less than we guaranteed in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Upon the prairie section of that road we guaranteed three-fourths of the cost not to_ exceed $13,000 per mile. The minister points out certain inconveniences. These inconveniences have not been to the. country, but to the persons who are building the road. We are supposed to be looking at it here at least to some extent from the country's standpoint. What is the evidence upon which the minister asks this committee to come to the conclusion that that road will cost $50,000 per mile upon the average, and that, therefore, $35,000 per mile is a reasonable amount to which the country should pledge its credit for the purpose of consummating the construction of the road?

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.

cost $15,000 or $20,000 or $30,000 or $100,000 per mile. Therefore, I am obliged to .rely on the reports of experts who do know. The minister is handicapping his own case before the committee, by not coming here armed with evidence of that kind. If I were trying to put a proposition of this kind through a committee of this House,^ it would be the first thing that I would think of. I would not expect the committee to pay any attention to me when I asked them to assume that this road would cost $50,000 a mile, and to base their action upon that assumption unless I had provided them with evidence or a report indicating what the road would cost.

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY-GUARANTEE OF BONDS.
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend
does not see it from my viewpoint.
