Under the present arrangement for crossing a highway special application has to be made to the board. This is to provide that the board may give a general order under general conditions by which a wire can be laid across.
Why should that not apply to telephone wires as well as to electrical energy wires?

I do not see why the Railway Board cannot have their engineers design a standard form of crossing for telephone and telegraph wires, because it is a great hardship to compel small independent telephone lines to appear before the board ana go to the expense of drawings and all that kind of thing. A telegraph wire is not nearly as dangerous as a telephone wire, and the minister would be justified in including telephone wires in this clause.
Even though there are standard conditions, should the railway company object, application will still have to be made to the board. I suppose the railway company would invariably object.

In nine cases out of ten the companies do not object now, but the chairman of the board thought it wise to leave in that provision in case some special condition might arise. I cannot just now see what objection there is to adding telephone wires, but I will let the clause stand and make inquiry.
On section 9-waterpipes.
In this case also the consent of the railway company is necessary. Could not the onus be put on the railway company to formulate the objection?
I would prefer to leave the clause stand as the board has arranged it, and we can see how it works out.

In former day3 the railway companies always objected, and it was only when Mr. MeGuigan became a power in the Grand Trunk that a farmer was allowed to drain his land across the railway track. He took the ground that if the farmer could raise an extra bushel of

grain on the land to be drained the railway company would have that much more crop to haul. This has been a very contentious matter. What is the law now?

The Board of Railway Commissioners has the power to allow these pipes to be placed on application of the parties, and this clause provides a certain standard method under which the pipes can be laid without application to the board, if no objection is raised.
On section 10-fencing right of way.
M.r' GRAHAM. Hon. gentlemen from the west will have interest in this clause. It is not easy to frame a law on this matter which will apply equally to the older sections of the Dominion as to the new This clause has received the attention of the Railway Commissioners, and it has been discussed with the representatives of the western farmers in the desire to reasonably meet their views. This clause seems to meet the difficulty fairly well, and has practically been agreed to. The present law relieves the company from fencing unless the board orders them to fence, and we are reversing this, and saying that they shall have to fence unless the board relieves them from the obligation.
We contended for that in 1903 when the Railway Act was passed.
Suppose the board should make an order relieving the company permanently, not temporarily, has the board power to vary that order? '
The board has that power under the general Act, and they use it frequently.
They vary their orders every day just as they deem fit.

Under subsection 5, where a, railway is being constructed through inclosed land it shall be the duty of the company to take effective measures to prevent cattle, and other animals escaping from such inclosed land on the property of the company. That is all right as far as it goes; but if a railway company is building through a field of wheat and the contractors working for the company see fit to throw down the fences, the railway company claims that there is no responsibility on its part. I know a case in which under such circumstances a man lost his entire crop. That should be from vided for.
Would that make them liable for the action of the contractor?

I would like to see the clause put in snch shape that the company must settle for the damages in two weeks, because I know cases in which the companies have been humbugging with settlers. How does the settler proceed to secure his remedy?

I suppose he can only have the ordinary 'recourse of suing for damages. The trouble, as I understood it, irom the complaints made to me, was that settlers would have their fences thrown down, and cattle would get in and destroy their crops, and the company would not be responsible. We try to make them responsible whether they do that or permit it to be done.

I know it is a serious question. You get contractors rushing through and building a railway, and they are not at all considerate of" the people whose lands they go through. I know instances where crops have been damaged and the owners have not been able to get any redress, even from the Railway Commission.
. ^r* DOHERTY. I do not think the wording suggested by the minister would exactly meet the case mentioned by the hon. member from Medicine Hat. It makes the company responsible for anything that is done or permitted to be done by the company. A case might arise where the company, in making its contract, would stipulate with the contractor that he must keep the fences in order, and must refrain from doing anything that would permit the cattle to escape. The company in that case would say, we did not permit that to be done, hut did our best to prevent it; it is the action of an independent contractor. If it is intended to make the company responsible for the negligence of its agents or contractors, that should be provided for by express words.
The section provides that the company shall take effective measures to prevent.

But it goes on to limit the obligation of the company to prevent by the words ' by reason of any act done or permitted to be done by the company.' I am not prepared to say that under that wording the company would not be responsible if the contractors did it; but if the intention is to make it clear that the company

is to be responsible for the contractors meglect, I would suggest that you make it read: ' done or permitted to be done by the company or by any agent or contractor acting for it.'

Might I make a suggestion? Strike out the words ' to take effective measures ' so that the clause will read ' it shall be the duty of the company to prevent cattle, &c/ That makes the du y absolute upon the company.

As the minister is leaving a number of these sections over, he might probably leave this one also, and the hon. member for St. Anne division (Mr. Doherty) could draft a clause. There has been great difficulty arising out of this very matter of the independent contractors. I have had cases in which I could not recover from the railway company on that account. The minister is anxious to get a remedy, and we might frame a section in the meantime.
What I was trying to accomplish was not only to protect the farmers against loss from the killing of stock, but also from injury to crops by the cattle going through them.

I would suggest that clause 5 should read:
Where the railway is being constructed through inclosed lands, the company shall prevent cattle and other animals escaping from such inclosed lands upon the property of the company.
The objection to that would be that it would only prevent their getting on the company's land and they might get into some other fellow's field.
I would suggest to strike out the last three words ' permitted by the company ' and substitute ' done or omitted to be done by the company, its servants, agents, contractors ot workingmen.'

I hope the company will be able to arrange this matter so that a clause of this kind may become law. The grievance is a very serious one, especially in the county I represent, as the railway companies are killing horses and cattle there almost every week in the year. Sometimes they kill them in bunches of a dozen head at a time: and in the last few years they have refused compensation of any kind. I would like to know particularly whether, if the railway board, under subclause 4 of section 10, should relieve a company from putting in cattle guards or building fences, would the company then be responsible for stock running at large and being killed?

My hon. friend will find that provided for in the next clause. How -would it do to accept the suggestion of the Mr. DOHERTY
hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) subject to discuss again in committee and add the words ' done or omitted to be done by the company, its agents, contractors or servants '?

That throws the onus on the owner of the land to prove that the company threw down the fences and let the cattle get in on the land. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) made the best suggestion, putting the absolute duty on the railway company, of preventing damage.
Suppose a man not connected with the railway should throw down a fence, the railway would be held responsible?

That is the view which accounts for the words ' effective measures being in the proposed amendment. I suggested making it very drastic, but the Justice Department thought I should only make the railway company responsible for their own acts and not for other people's acts.

I do not agree with the hon. minister. When contractors take a contract from a railway company, they employ all kinds of people, and those men are passing in and out of one's property when building the road through it. Some one should be responsible for these men. If they should throw down a gate or tear down a fence at night, some one should be made responsible to the owner. If the minister allows this clause to stand over, I would suggest that he give it more thought and let us have an opportunity to .discuss the proposed amendment again. If contractors undertake to build a railway and go on my property, they should see that my property is protected.

I would like to call attention to this case. Suppose cattle escape, through the negligence of the company, from inclosed lands on to other property, and then escape on to still further property, would the clause cover that?

I think it would. It was intended to make the company responsible for whatever might result from their action or omission.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 11,
11. Sections 294 and 295 of the principal Aoc, and sections 8 and 9 of chapter 50 of the Statutes of 1910, are repealed, and the following is enacted as section 294 of the principal Act:
294. The company shall be liable to the owner for the full value of all horses, sheep, swine or other cattle that may be killed or injured upon the company's lands through the opera-

tion of the railway, save where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person-
(a)	failing to keep the gates at any farm crossing, at each side of the railway closed, when not in use; or,
(b)	leaving open any gate on either side of the railway provided for the use of any farm crossing without some competent person being at or near such gate to prevent animals passing through such gate on to the railway; or.
(c)	other than an officer, contractor, or employee of the company, taking down any part of the railway fence; or,
(d)	turning any animal upon or within the enclosure of any railway company; or,
(e)	except as authorized by this Act, without the consent of the company, riding, leading or driving any animal, or suffering it to enter upon any railway and within the fences and guards thereof; or,
(f)	leaving the gates of the company at railway stations open for the convenience of the public.

This clause has the approval of the Farmers5 Association as it is now drawn:
The company shall he liable to tbe owner for the full value of all horses, sheep, swine or other cattle that may be killed or injured upon the company's lands through the operation of the railway, save where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person.
Then it gives the exceptions. It repeals absolutely the clause which provides that cattle shall not run at large on the highways within half a mile of a railway. The exceptions are just as they were in the old Act with one added-relating to gates at railway stations left open for the convenience of the public-the company is not held liable for cattle going in through these gates. With the exceptions made in the Bill the railway company is liable in all cases.

This is a very important section. Cases under it arise in every part of the Dominion. I would suggest that this section be allowed to stand until we have an opportunity to look into it. There are words at the close of this section that, I think, should not be there, the words, ' any person.' The effect of the section is to provide that the Tailway shall not be liable for cattle killed if the killing is caused by reason of ' any person ' leaving the gate open. It does not confine it to the owner of the premises. Might not a stranger, in walking through a man's farm, leave the gate open so that the cattle might get out and get killed? Yet, in that case the railway would not be responsible.
Are they to be responsible for the acts of a person with whom they have no connection?

I think that under the Act as it is now the railway
company is liable unless it can show negligence on the part of the owner. The onus is on the railway company.

The people who are most interested agreed to this. It took me some weeks to get a Bill that would be drastic and yet acceptable, and, having reached that point, I would not like to change it if it can be avoided.
It might be a question whether the neighbour who leaves the gate open should not be responsible for damages.
It would be all right to make it apply to the owner of the land or his servant. But if it would apply in the case of ' any person ' as is proposed here-I would not go so far as that.

This question of farm crossings is very involved and difficult, but when a railway company goes through a property, and creates a nuisance, the liability properly rests upon them for keeping the fences in order.
It is the Tailway fence, and they should keep it closed. The only thing that should deprive the owner of compensation is the leaving of the gate open by himself or his servant.

That would be carrying the responsibility -of the railway company altogether too far. The Tailway is in the public interest, but it is in liis own interest the farmer gets the gate. If the railway company were called upon to undertake the keeping of all such gates closed the expense would be enormous. The farmer who gets the gate usually takes upon himself the duty of seeing that it is kept closed, and he should not allow other people to open it. It is his business to keep it closed.

I do not agree with the hon. member (Mr. Barker), that the farmer gets the gate for his convenience. The farmer has his farm, and the railway company runs through it. The railway company must put up the fence, and it is right that the farmer should be, as far as possible, left in the condition he was in before. I think the only burden on the farmer should be that he shall not neglect to close his gate, but if any stranger or employee of the railway company should leave the gate open, the railway should be responsible. They create the condition of things that makes it dangerous. The farmer should be responsible only for the actions of himself and his servants or agents in these matters. .

I agree largely with 1/he hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), though I do not go quite so far as he does. I agree partially with the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), that ' any

person ' might include the railway servants, which it ought not to do. If the railway's servants leave the gate open- which, by the way, they sometimes do-the railway should be responsible, but for any other person the farmer should he responsible, for it is his duty to see that the gate is kept shut.

I would like to add this, and I am sure the Minister of Eailways will consider it. We here must think not merely of the loss to the farmer in having cattle killed, but also of the more important consideration of the safety of trains. If every farmer along a thousand miles of railway might, without risking personal loss, leave his gate open negligently, trusting to the duty of the railway company to keep his gates closed, we should have plenty of railway accidents, for gates could be left open, cattle would go upon the track and be run into, and trains would be thrown off the track.

No one should be on the railway track unless he is a servant of the railway company, and if such a man goes through a farmer's property, and leaves the gate open the railway company should be liable. The railway company has the privilege of arresting anybody for trespassing on its property.

It seems to me that the difficulty could he overcome by the farmer putting a lock on the gate. I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), that it would he unreasonable to ask that the railway he held responsible.

This section was an important point, but I think it was pretty well considered. I think it is not a breach of confidence to say that the chairman of the Eailway Commission was strongly of the view that it would save many cattle if a clause weTe put in the Act to fine every farmer who leaves his gate open. I could not go quite so far. A railway runs through a man's farm, and he gets damages. He wants a crossing, and makes application to the board. But the board is very fair to the farmers in giving them crossings. I would insist always that the gate shall be kept closed by the farmer or his assistants or your transportation might be ruined as well as the farmer's stock killed, but I will go as far as any person to make the railways responsible for their neglect to protect the farmer's cattle. But there is a certain liability on the part of the owner of stock from which he should not be relieved altogether. I do not think the farmers would appreciate our saying that they had no responsibility at all. The chairman of the board had strong views on that point, and the farmers themselves are willing to assume all just liabilities for their own actions.
Mr. NESBITT

When this Bill is passed I presume it refers only to the owners of cattle and property through which the railway runs. We have had cases in the west where the cattle of a man who owned land half a mile from the railway, finding the fences down, strayed away on to the railway. This Bill says the company shall be liable to the owner for the full amount of the cattle killed or injured. Where a man owns cattle a mile away from the railway, and they stray on the railway and are killed, does this law allow him compensation?
This law would allow him compensation. I imagine it would not if his cow was killed at a crossing, but if anywhere else on the track, he would get compensation.
According to the present law I do not think he does receive compensation.
That is the old law.

This Act repeals the clause which says that cattle shall not he left running at large within half a mile of a railway. That was made for the west where cattle grazed beside the track, and was the source of vexation. Then the railway must pay full compensation to every person whose cattle are killed, except in the circumstances named here.
Under the old law cattle running at large and getting upon another man's land were trespassers, and the trespassing owner had no right as against the railway company, and could not recover.
If the cattle were at large within half a mile of the track, the railway had a defence to put up.

It might meet the case by striking out the word ' person ' in the clause which says ' where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person,' and make it read * by reason of any owner, or railway company, or their agents, servants or workmen failing to keep the gates' closed.' That would make it equally the duty of the farmer and the railway company to keep the gates shut.
The railway company is not responsible for keeping a farmer's gates shut.
I suggest to add, after the word ' person,' ' any person excepting the company or their servants.'

I understand from the minister that if the gates are left open, and cattle are killed, the farmer will get nothing for his cattle. But supposing those cattle cause the wreck of a train or dam-

age to a train, would the farmer be liable for that?

We passed an Act last year to make that clear. Would these words be acceptable ' Where such killing or injury is caused by reason of any person not being an employee or agent of the company ' ? Personally I feel that in the interests of those most affected we might as well not pass the item at all as not meet the views on which all were agreed. It wms agreed by all parties that this was a solution of the difficulty.
On section 12, correction of clerical errors.

The provision in section 12:
No action shall lie against the company by reason of anything in any policy of insurance or by reason of payment of any moneys thereunder,
is unfair legislation.
There is no new legislation in this section, that is already on the statute-books.
I think it is bad legislation.

The matter wes dealt with by a special committee last year which met representatives of the railway companies and others concerned, and this clause was agreed upon. There would be a good deal of dissatisfaction if it were changed now.
The railway companies were represented on the committee but not the insurance companies. I was on the committee.

Everybody was represented who should be.
On section 13, Railway Commission and electrical power.

We have given the Board of Railway Commissioners, power to say at what price power- generated from water-powers under Dominion jurisdiction shall be furnished. This gives them power to issue orders as to the quantity to be furnished.

Subsection 2 provides machinery to ascertain the quantity whether they have a sufficient quantity. Should that not also apply to subsection 3 so that they can ascertain whether the company need all the power for their own use?

The reason for that is that we have leased many powers to companies solely for their own use. This is to provide that it shall not be possible for
any one to demand of them power which they have not even a right to dispose of.
On section 14, government aided railways falling into bad repair.

This is an important and drastic amendment. In Canada we have granted aid very liberally towards railways. Cases have been brought to my notice where railways liberally aided by the parliament of Canada have allowed their roads to become so delapidated that a train cannot be run safely on them. In some cases the rails have been taken up and we have had the spectacle of a road that the people have helped to construct vanishing as old rails, the receipts being obtained by the owners of the road. The railways are aided for the purpose of giving the people transportation and it ought to be our view to have that object carried out even at the expense of the country. This section provides that where a company under federal jurisdiction has been aided by the Dominion parliament and its road becomes unfit to operate, this aid becomes a first lien on that road, and the Board of Railway Commissioners, at the request of the minister, can practically foreclose that first lien, sell the road or dispose of it and use the funds to put it in proper condition, something to get the people the use of the road for which they paid. The objection has been raised that it is dangerous legislation to say that the aid given as a gift by the parliament of Canada should be allowed to become an underlying charge, even under the firi.t mortgage bonds. There is a good deal of force in that argument, but there is this reply, that a road which gets into that condition does not give any value to its first mortgage bonds or any other bonds, and the only way for the railway to be made of any use to the people or value to the bondholders is to have it put in proper condition. The object of this is to practically give the government power to take possession of these roads it has aided and see they are put in proper condition for the use of the people.
Has the minister anv such railway in his mind that he could mention?
I would not care to mention them, because if I were wrong it would be unfair to the railways. This clause will, I think, be a mighty lever to have these railways put in a fit condition to operate.

I had in mind the branch line from Madoc to Eldorado, which was subsidized by the federal government and the municipalities through which it runs and has not been operated for a number of years. The hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) made an effort to have this

road operated, but without success. Would this clause compel the railway company to operate that road?
If the road is unfit to be operated on account of its condition, means are provided here to put it in proper con-[DOT] dition, but I am not sure it would compel operation.
It may be confiscated.
Well, disposed of.
There ought to be some provision foT notifying the bondholders before the road is closed up.
All interested parties would, I suppose, be notified by the board.
This clause does not cover the case of the railway I have mentioned.
I do not think it does.

Would it not be well to take power to compel the operation of that and other such railways? This line has been subsidized, but it has not been operated for a number of years, and no other company will undertake to build in that territory, because if they did the Grand Trunk would lilkely commence to operate the Madoc and Eldorado branch line. In such cases it would be well to empower the board to take action.
There is a good deal in the suggestion of the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) that the first notice should go to the bondholders.
We will amend the clause so as to read that the trustees of the bondholders, if any, shall be notified.
What does the minister think of the suggestion regarding the case I have mentioned?
I think we had better not try to enlarge the scope of the Bill at present.

If a road gets into that condition, it is because it is not a paying proposition, and I do not think there is much use in attempting to put it into proper condition unless you are prepared to provide that it must be operated.
On section 15,

I wish to move that in the first line of section 372 after the word 'annually' there be inserted the words 'or more frequently if the minister so requires.' Heretofore the companies have been required to make returns semi-annually of certain accidents. As a matter of fact, they only make them annually. I am making it legal for them to make the returns annually for our general report be-
cause we only issue it annually, but I am providing that on the request of the minister they shall make them more frequently, and I propose to include with other accidents, the killing of animals.

Amendment agreed to, and section 15 as amended agreed to.
On section 16,

I have a section which I want to substitute for this. At the present time, when a railway company proproposes to change its tariff, it has to give only ten days' notice. I am asking that subsection 3 of section 328 be amended by striking out the word 'ten' and substituting the word 'thirty.' The meaning of that is that the railway company will be compelled to give thirty days' notice instead of ten.
Amendment agreed to.

As the object of this Bill is to straighten out a good many matters that are not very straight just now, I wish to mention that in connection with the building of the Transcontinental railway lands have been taken from the former owners and are now being used for the railway without having been paid for. An ordinary railway company has to make a deposit in court before it can go into occupation of lands so taken. It is not so with the Transcontinental railway. Besides the provision in the Transcontinental Railway Act for the expropriation of lands, there are conferred upon the commissioners all the rights that are given to a railway company under the Railway Act and its amendments. Proceedings have been taken in the Exchequer Court, and Judge Cassels, I believe, has held, in the case of King vs. Jones, that the proper proceeding is to proceed under the provisions of the Railway Act, and not under the Expropriation Act, and in the Exchequer Court. The Deputy Minister of Justice, I believe, differs from the judge, and the case is now in appeal, I believe, before the Supreme Court.
I understand that it has been decided that the Exchequer Court has jurisdiction, reversing the judgment.

In that case I beg the minister's pardon. That will relieve us from the difficulty. In the neighbourhood of Winnipeg a great many cases were held up, and hundreds of thousands of dollars, I believe, were not paid to the claimants. If the matter had remained as it was, I was going to ask for the insertion of a declaratory section in this Bill so as to relieve the difficulty.

I would like to inquire of the minister whether there has been

any complaint to -any great extent in regard to the operation of the provisions of the law in dealing with claims for damages for the killing of animals on railways. The practice now is to take such claims 'before the Railway Commission instead of as formerly before the local courts, and there has been in my section of the country a great deal of complaint of delay in consequence. Has there been any complaint of that kind made or is the new regulation operating to advantage?

I have a great deal of complaint from western Canada but none from eastern Canada. The complaint from western Canada arises out of the belief that the railway companies kill cattle and horses and then their employees immediately bury them, so that a farmer, after hunting for months, will discover his stock beneath the sod. It is said that the railway companies dispute all and sundry claims, and it is very difficult for a farmer under the circumstances to prove his allegation.
If the local courts had jurisdiction, at the expense of some $5 or $10, a farmer could bring his action and have his case tried, whereas now the cost and trouble are prohibitory.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the jurisdiction of the local courts is taken away?
Yes. Suppose a farmer has a cow killed on a railway, instead of going to a division court he has to apply to the Railway Commission.
What section of the Act compels him to do that?
I have not the section, but that is the practice. As soon as a claim is made on a railway company, which they dispute, they say it has to go to the Railway Commission.
In that they are wrong.
That is the practice.
People go to the Railway Commission because they think they can get speedier justice.

A year ago we changed the Act relating to the Intercolonial railway to provide that the ordinary law shall apply to the Intercolonial railway, and thus enable claimants for damages on account of cattle killed on the government's railway to go to the ordinary court, as they would in the case of cattle killed on an ordinary railway.

I know of many cases, such as described by my hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Porter), of animals killed, and the railway companies simply laughed
at the claims for compensation. I never heard any complaint made regarding the change from the common courts to the Railway Board because the railway companies have absolutely refused to pay damages of any kind. These companies killed at least 50 animals within a few miles of my home within the last few years and refused to pay damages of any kind.

I would be surprised to learn that such an amendment to the Railway Act was enacted because I had a couple of suits last year for loss of cattle which I won in the ordinary courts. It would be very extraordinary if there was such an amendment because that would deprive us of a right to a jury trial, and jury trials are very effective against railway companies.

I would like to draw attention to clause (5) in section 11:
The company shall be liable to the owner for the full value of all horses, swine, sheep or other cattle.
I think that the words 'other animals' should be substituted for 'other cattle,' so as to cover every class of animal likely to be damaged. There is one valuable class of animals plentiful in the country and I do not think you could collect under this clause.

If my hon. friend will look at the interpretation clause of the Act he will find that the word 'cattle' is a very comprehensive term and includes everything except those animals specifically mentioned in that clause.
Progress reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved third reading of Bill (No. 213) to amend the Bank Act.

I find in the schedule the name of the Farmers' Bank, of Canada. That charter, I understand, is to be completed along with others although the bank is practically out of business. What effect will this legislation have on the Farmers' Bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That point has been carefully considered. I am advised by the law officers that this amendment leaves matters exactly as they are. Whatever rights any party has with regard to the Farmers' Bank remain undisturbed.
form. The Department of Justice advised that it was expedient to put in the name for that purpose.

I would call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the desirability of appointing a Royal Commission to inquire thoroughly into the conditions of banks in this country and other countries with the view of improving our present Banking Act. Recent events have disclosed many serious defects in it. The provisions regarding government inspection do not meet with the approval of many people. The provision in the Bill brought down, would not meet the approval of many people outside the bank authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure that they approve it.
I do not think . they would raise any serious objections to it. I should imagine it should meet with their approval.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not emanate from them.

I am glad to hear that because I was under the impression it had been drafted by the counsel of the Bankers' Association, or some one standing close to them. 1 do not think that our banks pay enough for the great privileges they enjoy. In France, England and Germany the banks pay the government for the privilege of issuing currency. Under our system they pay nothing. There should be some restraint, some taxation, should be placed on the right to send money out of the country for speculative purposes. All these and a great many other important matters should be thoroughly investigated by a commission and reported to our next narliament. For when the Bank Act is before the commission what may we expect? We shall have bank presidents and inspectors presenting their views, but no one to speak on behalf of the people. If we had a Royal Commission to examine and report, it might make many suggestions which would assist us to come to a proper conclusion. In the Toronto 'Telegram' of May 16, I find this despatch from Washington:
Washington, D.C., May 16.-Out of a total expenditure to date of $207,130 to study the various banking systems of the world, with a view to improving the United States banking laws, the National Monetary Commission has spent $2,931 to learn about Canadian banks.
Here we have the United States people spending $200,000 in investigating the banking conditions of other countries, and we have not had a Royal Commission to investigate the banking system of our own country. There are_ patent and admitted defects in our banking law, as shown by
Mr. FIELDING
the many failures that have occurred. I think it would be well to spend if necessary $20,000 or $30,000 to have a commission investigate thoroughly the conditions in Canada and other countries, and report next session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Fortunately, the desire to improve-where it may be improved

the Bank Act is one which hon. members on both sides will share. Therefore, any suggestion looking to that end Will be received by the government with all the ' consideration to which it is entitled. I frankly say that I doubt whether a Royal Commission would serve the good purpose my hon. friend (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario) has in view. To begin with, it would be rather difficult to get the right kind of men to serve on a Royal Commission for that purpose, men who have the capacity, knowledge and experience necessary. To a large extent-not conclusively-we must learn from the experienced bankers themselves. We are not bound to accept their suggestions, but they are certainly well qualified to give us information and useful advice. I do not reject the hon. gentleman's proposal for a Royal Commission, but at first glance I doubt whether it will serve the purpose.
There was one to investigate life insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was for a different condition of affairs. The hon. member will recollect that there had been an outbreak in the United States in regard to the insurance companies of that country, and many irregularities had been disclosed. A feeling of distrust arose with regard to our own companies. I think, notwithstanding some things that occurred which became the subjects of controversy, it was the wise thing to have an inquiry into our insurance laws, and their operation, in order to reassure the public of Canada as to the stability of our insurance companies. At any rate, that was the reason for the commission. I do not think a similar condition exists with regard to our banks. Our banking system, while not a perfect success yet,
I think, in the opinion of many of the financial men of the world is held to be a good system. Other countries seek information from us and learn irom us.
Touching the question of taxation, it is a common view that the banks should be taxed to a larger degree. That is worthy of consideration. But it must be remembered that the country needs banking capita] to facilitate trade, and that if you have too many restrictions upon banks and the organization of banks, you will never get the banking capital needed. When you consider there is a double liability of shareholders, the responsibility the bank direc-

tors have to assume ' with all the obligations now imposed upon shareholders and directors, I am inclined to think that if you enforce substantial taxes upon them you may defeat the purpose the hon. gentleman has in view. However, these are only passing thoughts. I quite appreciate the interest the hon. gentleman has taken in the subject, and I will discuss his suggestions with my colleagues in due course.

I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario), who favours the appointment of a Royal Commission on this subject. I went carefully over the results of the work of the commission in the United States, and it seemed to me that they had collated a lot of very valuable information, which will, if made known to the people of Canada, and especially to the parliament of Canada, would afford us useful lessons in amending our Banking Act. Our banking system is generally regarded as a very good one. But I am far from being of the opinion that it is entitled to the eulogies very frequently expended upon it. I do not think our banking system has fulfilled what the country might reasonably have expected of it. The Minister of Finance says we must learn from the bankers. The experience of the bankers will teach us much if we can get it set forth frankly. But we must learn much more from the great public as well. The public are not being served as they should be by our banking system. Here is a case that is known to me: One of the regular banks of Canada has a branch in a certain town. A farmer living within a mile and a quarter of that branch bank, a man well known to the manager of the bank, the owner of a fine farm of about 200 acres with good buildings and not a dollar of debt on the property, a man having debts of not more than $200 in the world, a sober, industrious man who has always enjoyed the reputation of being reliable and prompt in meeting his obligations-when that man asked the bank manager for the loan of $25 he was refused. Why? Because he would not get an endorser. To that bank as to others, parliament- has given great privileges-it can stamp paper and call it bank notes, and earn interest on it from the day it goes out, and many other privileges it has from which it makes money. The people must use the banks, because the banks hold the circulating medium which they must hold to carry on business. Yet this is the way one man was used. I asked the manager why, and his answer was: Our instructions from headquarters are to discount no notes no matter how good the individual may be unless he gets an endorser.
Look at our banks to-day. What has built these palatial banking houses that we see on every corner? Pass along Sparks street
or Bank street in this city, pass along King or Yonge street in Toronto, and how many hundreds of thousands, and even millions, of dollars you find invested in costly buildings for the banks. These have been built out of the earnings of the people who pay very sweetly for any business they do with the banks.
Then, go behind the counters of the banks and look at the employees. Consider the long hours they have to serve. We had a discussion on the Bill introduced by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Lewis), and since that time I have had two or three letters from parties whose sons are employed in these banks, telling of the long hours they have to work-extending in some instances to eleven and even twelve o'clock at night. One man tells me of his son working until nine o'clock at night without anything to eat-the work had to be finished. And yet that boy works for only $4.75 a week. For what purpose? That they may be able to pay dividends of 9, 10, 11 and 12 and 13 per cent to their stockholders. Would y.ou call that a banking system that is to be admired? What is our banking system? The great central banks send out their dicta to the branches that must be obeyed, everything must be done the same as at headquarters. The branch manager knows the conditions of the locality where his bank is situated, he knows the wants of the people, whereas the head office knows nothing about them; -still the branches have to take their orders from headquarters. Compare that with the American system, which is called a bad banking system. There a bank starts in a small village, it accepts the savings of the people, and loans, them out to the industries of the country, to the manufacturers and other people, who need money to pay their workmen. The money thus loaned out serves to develop industries in that locality. Compare that with the Canadian system. Here the banks take the savings from the hard working people, and their money immediately goes to the head office, to be transferred very likely down to Wall Street to be used in stock speculations, because they can earn more on it than they can at home. I can point out line after line where our banking system is defective. I Temember when a branch of the Central Bank was started in Durham. The manager of that bank told me that every time he got a few thousand dollars even though it was not half enough to meet the needs of the people in his locality, a demand came from headquarters, and that money went away to be invested in New York. The people who had saved the money and put it into the bank could not get the advantage of it. Then there is the low rate of interest upon the savings of the people.

The banks are strong enough to control this government, and the rate of interest in the government savings banks is put at the same figure as in the private banks, compelling the people to deposit their money with the government at three per cent interest because they can get no more from it anywhere else. I think the banks should be made useful institutions to the public here as they are in England, France and Germany, where they take up the earnings of the people and lend them out again at a higher rate of interest than they can get in the ordinary banks. Such a system puts a premium on industry, on frugality, and economy, by giving the people a larger rate of interest than they get in the banks to-day. Some years ago we were paying depositors four per cent in the government savings banks, but twice since I came into this House the Finance Minister cut down the rate of interest. At whose instance? At the instance of the banks. They appeal to the people to put their money into the bank and only give them three per cent; but when they go to borrow it for their needs they have to pay seven and eight per cent. Is that a proper service rendered to the public by the banks, to whom we give charters? I say many such evils as I have referred to would be brought out by a royal Commission, that would enable us to consider them carefully and provide a remedy. When we amend the Bank Act, if we had a royal commission, it would afford us the needed information	upon	which	we	couldbase a	remedy for	the	evils
complained of. The representatives of the people do not, in many cases, know how serious these evils are, and they could be brought out by a royal commission in a better way than any other. There are many others that I might refer to. Take the banks of France, take the banks in Germany, take the Farmers' banks. They lend their money at a rate not above five per cent, and they pay a certain per cent to the government on the business they do. Whereas our banks are allowed' an unlimited right to earn what they can, and they pay the government nothing for the privilege. Now, with regard to another subject. A few years ago I read about the case of a young man, who was employed in one of these banks. He had been a steady young man for some years, he had been saving his earnings in view of a time when he could settle down His salary was about $900 a year. He took it into his head to get married, he married a very estimable young lady, and one who had means^ coming from her own people to assist him. But what was the result? That young man was dismissed from the bank inside three days after his wedding he did not wait until he had $1,000 salary. Is that not putting an
^ JHg0SPROULEarriaSe? IS that n0t
interference with the free rights of the people? I say no young man should be placed under such an embargo as that, at a time in life when he desires to get married, when nature and everything demands that he should settle down in wedded life. When the requirements of the state, the propagation of the species, when everything demands that he should marry, he is not allowed to do so. Some hon. members find this a laughing matter. But I say that it is a very serious matter. I have letters in my possession, and information which, in my judgment, show that this is a matter highly important to the country, one that should receive at our hands the most careful consideration. It is an evil that nothing short of a law, making it a criminal offence for any mapager of a bank to enforce such a rule upon his employees, will afford a remedy. It is not only a grievance, it is a cruel injustice, it is at least a moral crime against young men, many of whom could settle down and become even more valuable to the bank that employs them. But why don't the banks pay their employees a reasonable salary? Why do they.insist upon extracting from them every drop of blood they can draw out in the way of long hours and steady service, for a mere pittance, in order that they may show the world what large dividends they can pay? Do we not want information about these things? I think we want more information than we have, to enable us to loot into these matters very carefully when we come to amend the Bank Act, to see if we cannot provide a remedy against the crying evils that are prevalent to-day.

United States 41 per cent of the resources of the banks is applied to stocks and bonds, 12 per cent applied* to real estate, and only 23 per cent of the resources of the banks in the United States is applied to ordinary mercantile loans. In Canada we have no bank loans on real estate, because the law does not permit of it, but, 24 per cent of the resources of the Canadian banks is applied to stocks and bonds, and 51 per cent is applied to mercantile loans. (Eef. page 40.)
What do you mean by mercantile loans?

Ordinary commercial loans, ordinary business paper of all kinds, and not loans on stock or anything of that kind. In the United States the proportion applied to fostering the industries of the country, and the lending of money to ordinary individuals on theiir notes is only 23 per cent of the resources of the banks, whereas in the case of Canadian banks the percentage is 51 per cent. The banks of Canada lend proportionately over twice as much of their funds for the ordinary purposes of the community as do the banks of the United States.

Mr. FIELDING moved second reading of Bill (No. 219) to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act. He said: There are two old savings banks in the, province of Quebec whose charters wgje granted, I think, before confederation, and from time to time their charters are renewed in the same manner as the charters of the other banks. We propose to extend these charters for one year as in the case of the other banks. There is one other clause which enables them to re-arrange their stocks in shares of $100 which is a very desirable thing.
What rate of interest do they pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Three per cent.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, considered in committee and reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the third reading of the Bill.
Do these banks do an ordinary banking business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They do not issue notes. They are of high standing, and excellent reputation, and have power to loan money within certain limitations.

I believe there ought to be established all over the country banks for the purpose of taking the savings of Mr. PERLEY.
the people and paying a higher rate of interest on them than do the existing banks. I believe the state should make better provision for the handling of the money of those who can earn it but are not financiers enough to invest it profitably. I believe the state should put as high a premium as possible on frugality and industry. Other countries seem to do that and succeed with it, and we might well take a lesson from them. My hon. friend gave us a nice history of the failures of Canadian banks. I notice that it has been prepared by a banker, and the best side of it has been put out. I would like to have a man who had been in the business for a few years and dropped out of it to give the other side. I think it would not sound quite as favourable or look as rosy as it does. When he makes a comparison between the failures of Canadian banks and the failures of American banks, he very conveniently leaves out of the comparison the number of failures of national banks in the two countries. Over 25 per cent of all our banks, I think, have gone down in the last 25 or 30 years, whereas, speaking from memory, from 5 to 7 per cent have gone down in the United States. There was another statement with regard to the amount of money our banks put in circulation through manufacturers or merchants or others for the use of the people. I have lived in both countries, and have seen the operations of the banks in both, and I cannot believe from what I have seen and know that that statement is even approximately correct. If it is, it is only accounted for by this, that the large amounts of money put in circulation through large corporations like railway companies or wholesale men are put out in the great metropolitan centres, and not in the small towns and villages. In my judgment, the banks of the United States serve the people better than the banks here. In saying that, I am not especially enamoured of the banking system of the United States, which is defective in many respects, fairer comparison might have been made by comparing the Canadian banks with French or German or English banks. Another consideration in connection with the banking business that has always appealed to me is this. We give certain corporations power to handle the circulating medium of our country-what for? To supply that to the whole people of the country, and not simply to a few millionaire merchants or railway corporations or great manufacturing concerns; every honest and industrious man in this country ought to have some limited credit in these banks. I think I am within the mark when I say that not over 5 per cent of this people of this country can go to these banks and get accommodation. There are at least 99 per cent who are never served by the institu-

tions which the state provides for the service of the people. A system that does not do any better than that for the people of the country is not in my judgment the best that human ingenuity can devise. Why is it that private banks succeed so well in Canada? People will go to them and pay 10 or 12 per cent for accommodation when they cannot get it from the standard banks? As long as the banks maintain the custom of denying accommodation to the great bulk of the people so long will I contend that the banking system of our country is, comparatively speaking, a failure.

How would my hon. friend define by any provision of law what persons a bank should extend credit to, and what not? Also, how does he account for the fact that there is not in Ontario to-day one private bank to every ten that there were ten years ago?

I cannot go into that as I would like at present; but perhaps at another time I will give a good reason for it. I think the hon. gentleman has overstated the fact when he says there is not one to ten.

With respect to bank failures, I would like to ask the hon. member from East Grey to consider, what difference does it make what proportion of the banks fail? The real test is what percentage of the money does the public lose that it puts into the banks?

I think it makes- this difference. In the various centres of Canada we have only 25 banks that supply all the credit, whereas the country would perhaps need 25,000. We confine the business to these large banks which do not give the people the accommodation they are entitled to.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 85) respecting Forest Reserves and Parks.- Mr. Oliver.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This Bill was gone through when it was in Committee of the Whole on a previous occasion, but it was held in committee for the purpose of making a small addition to section 18 suggested by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty). Since then an amendment has been drafted which has been agreed to by the hon. member for St. Anne division (Mr. Doherty) and I would ask the committee to adopt it and let the Bill take its third reading. The amendment was for the purpose of requiring that regulations for the disposition of the natural resources in the 295
parks should come before parliament for approval just as in the case of regulations under the Dominion Lands Act. The following is the amendment:
That to section 18 be added the following proviso: Provided that any regulation made by the Governor in Council under subsection (b) of section 16 shall remain in force until the day immediately succeeding the day if prorogation of the session of parliament next after the date of such regulations and no longer, unless during the session such regulations be approved by both Houses.
Why confine it to that particular subsection?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because this subsection deals with natural resources.
Does this amendment correspond with the provision in the Dominion Lands Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I do not see much distinction in principle between this particular subsection and some of the others. Why make any distinction between (b) and (c) or (b) and (g)?
* Mr. OLIVER. The idea was that regulations which merely had to do with the conduct of the business of the parks peed not come before parliament, but that those having to do with the alienation of natural resources ought to have the approval of parliament.
There may be Some ground for such a distinction, but take subsection (g) which deals with the confiscation of property and disposal of the things seized. That is rather an important regulation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was not considered necessary that parliament should take responsibility regarding regulations for the administration of the parks, but that the alienation of the rights of the Crown in natural resources required the sanction of parliament.

If you are going to apply your amendment to subsection (b) you should divide that subsection into two, and confine your amendment to the cutting and removal of timber, the working of mines, quarries and mineral deposits, and make a new paragraph to include the removal of sand, gravel, &c., so that your amendment shall not apply to comparatively trivial things.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are all of the same class. There is the right to the use and [DOT]occupation of land. That deals with the occupation of land within the reserve.

I understand perfectly the explanation, but if a settler wants a



load of sand for the building of his house or a municipality wants a few loads of gravel, that should not require the approval of parliament.
Why should the amendment to section 18 not apply to section 17 also?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know, but that it might apply to subsections (b) and (c) of section 17. I do not know that it is well to cumber the administration by unnecessary references to parliament. At the same time, if the committee insists upon it, I would not seriously object.
It does seem to me that subsection (c) of section 17 is of equal if not greater importance in this respect than subsection (b) of section 16.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the wording in the amendment I handed to my hon. friend were left as typewritten without the reference to section 16, the matters in subsection (c) of section 17 would be covered.

Why not merely add a few words, so as to make the section read:
Provided that any regulations made by the Governor in Council under the provisions of this Act with respect to the matters mentioned in subsection (b) of section 16 of this Act and subsection (c) of section 17 of this Act shall remain in force until the day immediately succeeding the day of prorogation of the session of parliament next after the date of such regulations and no longer, unless during the session such regulations be approved by both Houses of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will accept that.
Amendment agreed to.

The other night when we were discussing this Bill reference was made to squatters, and I think there is a provision by which squatters are not allowed on the land of a forest reserve. But at page 9 of the schedules, referring to certain subdivisions, it says that they have been withdrawn owing to the presence of a squatter, and that the presence of this squatter will tend to protect the forest against fire. How is the minister so much in favour of this particular squatter when there is a provision in the Act to prohibit squatters from going into the forest reserves? -

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This squatter was in occupation before the reserve was located. The question is whether it is better policy to buy out his rights or to cut him out of the resefve. In this case it is thought better to cut him out of the reserve than to buy out his rights.
Bill as amended reported, and read the third time and passed.

Bill (No. 212) to amend the Water Carriage of Goods Act, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

This Bill was left in my care by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I understand it has been thoroughly examined and reported upon by the Committee of Marine and Fisheries. The Act in question was passed in the session of 1910, and the shippers, especially in the maritime provinces, have represented to the government that section 10 of the Act hampers them in their business of exporting lumber to Great Britain. Some fifty petitions which I hold in my hands were sent to the department, asking for the repeal of that clause, and for the amendment which I now propose. A special committee appointed two or three year3 ago on Marine and Fisheries sat and heard the interested parties, the shipping federation and the lumber exporters. The legislature of New Brunswick has also passed a resolution to the same effect. In the evidence taken by the committee with regard to this Bill, it is stated on page 7 that the lumber people of the United Kingdom have refused to accept a Bill of lading used under the present Act. The Bristol Timber Importers' Association unanimously resolved not to purchase any more lumber cargoes under existing conditions. On page 29 of the evidence will be found certain telegrams from large shippers of lumber asking for the repeal of clause 10. The lumber industries ask that they shall be at liberty to enter into a contract with ship-owners for a bill of lading with what is known as the eonclusive evidence clause in it, so that shipping companies who do not wish to give such a bill of lading need not do so. They represent that section 10 is in restraint of trade with regard to the carriage of wood goods. The chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) read a telegram addressed to a Liverpool firm by Price, Walker & Company, Limited, Gloucester, which I will read:
Dear Sirs,-Cargo per SS. 'Hersilia' at Sheet Harbour. The provisions which you suggest will not meet the requirements of the Bristol channel importers. We will net comtract without the clause which has been adopted by our association being embodied in the contract itself.
There are one or two communications of a similar nature which I need not quote.

The minister has been dealing with section 2 of the Bill, whieh I understood pretty well. I was

familiar with the legislation passed by the legislature of New Brunswick, and "some other protests that had been made against section 10 of the Act as it originally stood. Would the minister tell us what was the original form of subsection (a) of section 2?

The only change is the addition of the words after the word * animals,' ' lumber, deals and other articles described as wood goods.' Subsection (a) in the original Act contained this clause:
Including goods, wares, merchandise and articles of any kind whatsoever except live animals.
The object of this amendment is to exclude wood goods from the operation of the Act relating to water carriage of goods. The original Act, clause 9, prohibits the shipowner from relieving himself from certain kinds of liability for negligence, and this clause 9 includes those goods. It was stated on behalf of the shipowners that they were not in a position to measure the goods and to find out the superficial feet, that it would take a great deal of time and cause delay, and that to ascertain whether a certain plank or deal contained so many superficial feet, was impracticable. Consequently, they asked for a clause that would relieve them from the liability, provided they delivered the number of pieces that were received from the merchant. That is the meaning of clause 10 which was in the Act of last year. The merchants of New Brunswick, it appears, object to that system and wish to go back to the system in force in that province previously by which the shipowner made himself liable not only for the number of pieces but also for the actual measurement, for the number of superficial feet contained in those pieces, and they required the shipowner to sign a bill of lading that he would deliver on the other side a certain number of superficial feet. Often when he reached the other side, there would not be that quantity of superficial feet in the ship and the shipowner had to make up the difference. The shipowner was anxious to get rid of that liability and it was on behalf of the small shipowners in the maritime provinces that that clause was inserted. The effect of this Bill will be to put the law back where it was before and leave absolute freedom for the shipowner and merchant to make their own contract. If the merchant can pervail on the shipowner to sign a bill of lading for a certain number of superficial feet it will be for the shipowner to deliver that, but if he refuses he has to make his bargain with the merchant.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
